And what is stated here—"the body is composed of the five elements, on account of smell, moisture, heat, structure, and the provision of space, and because of the authority of <s>śruti</s>"—this itself, as it literally stands, should be accepted as the established doctrine.

children.text: yacca---"svaguṇānnopalabhanta indriyāṇi kasmāditicet" "saguṇānamindriyabhāvāt" ityatra "na śabdaguṇopalabdheḥ" ityuktam; tatrāpi śrotrendriyasya ākāśāpyāyitātvādāpyāyakaguṇasya tadguṇatāṃ paṭanailyapānīyasaurabhādivat prakalpoktamuttaram /
athavā yathāgamamāhaṅkārikatvamindriyāṇāmajānataścodye bhūtāpyāyitendriyapakṣe sthitvaivedamuttaraṃ gūḍhābhiprāyeṇa dadīya iti /
children.translated_text: Alternatively, to one who does not know from <s>āgama</s> (scripture) that the sense organs are products of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle), and who raises the objection standing within the view that the sense organs are nourished by the elements, this answer is given with a hidden intention.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati---bhavatā kimindriyaguṇopalambhābhāva ucyate, kiṃ vā tadāpyāyakaguṇopalambhābhāvaḥ ? pūrvatrāṅgīkāra evottaram, śabdādīnāmanindriyaguṇatvāt /
children.translated_text: What is meant is this: do you mean the non-perception of the sense organ's own quality, or the non-perception of the quality of that which nourishes it? In the former case, the answer is already conceded, since sound and the rest are not qualities of the sense organs [themselves].
In the latter case, there is a deviation [from the rule].
Therefore, there is no occasion for conflict with <s>Vedānta</s>.

And regarding what is stated—in the passage "why do the sense organs not perceive their own qualities?" [answered by] "because of being sense organs possessing qualities," it is said "because of the perception of the quality of sound"—there too, the response has been devised that since the auditory organ is nourished by <s>ākāśa</s>, the quality of the nourishing [element] is [treated as] its own quality, like the fragrance of cloth, oil, and water.
And the objection regarding composite entities should be handled by the principle already stated.
The fifth [<s>adhyāya</s>], however, being exhausted by mere <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder) and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat), does not contribute anywhere to the ascertainment of reality.

The elegance and inelegance of deliberation as an auxiliary to practical discourse, however, should be disregarded by those learned in the science of examining real definitions, proper characterizations, and reasoning, since it merely follows the state of things as they are.

children.text: yat punararvāgbhirakṣacaraṇapañcādhyāyyāṃ kuśakāśāvalambena kaṇacaraṇakathāṃ niveśya naigamikyaḥ padavyo nirudhyante, tatra tu nūnaṃ sa eva gautamaḥ svayamantaḥ prahasati //
children.translated_text: As for the later [commentators] who, in the five-chapter [work] of <s>Akṣacaraṇa</s> (i.e., <s>Akṣapāda</s>), forcibly insert the doctrine of <s>Kaṇacaraṇa</s> (i.e., <s>Kaṇāda</s>) by grasping at straws and obstruct the traditional paths of interpretation—in that case, surely <s>Gautama</s> himself laughs inwardly!

In the fourth <s>adhyāya</s>—the examination of activity, attachment, aversion, and so forth; the demonstration of the afterlife and so on through the eternality of the <s>ātman</s> (self); and the examination of causeless origination, the doctrine that everything is non-eternal, and the doctrine that everything is eternal—all this is extremely concordant [with our view].
Thus [ends] the position of acceptance.

children.text: yadvā nātīva ca bahiṣkāro nātīva ca parigrahaḥ /
children.translated_text: Alternatively: neither too much rejection nor too much acceptance;
as with <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and the rest, here too the approach should be "the grain husked to satisfaction."
On account of the preponderance of what is serviceable, [the <s>Nyāya-sūtras</s> merit] inclusion among the <s>vidyāsthānas</s> (branches of knowledge);
the exclusion [applies] only to those portions in the <s>sūtras</s> and the like that are contradictory.
<s>Nyā</s>. <s>Pa</s>. <s>Pra</s>. 4.
Determination of the qualified student.
And this elaboration of logic (<s>Nyāyavistara</s>) has a restricted qualification [of students].
And from [having] a restricted qualification, this elaboration of logic is as follows.
The compassionate one (<s>Gautama</s>) taught the <s>śāstra</s> out of [its] greatness, there being no [ultimate] harm [from its study].
To say that it is open to all is a statement made without due consideration.
How can those who have not studied <s>āgama</s> (scripture) know the matters of <s>āgama</s>?
Or how would one be compassionate if one were urging them toward what is prohibited?
Nor can the harm be averted by inferences such as the purificatory power of a human skull and the like.
Abandoning <s>āgama</s> and [relying on] perception and the rest, there is a twofold disruption even there:
for in <s>śruti</s> (Vedic scripture), due to the lack of qualification [of <s>śūdras</s>], and in other [sources], due to the lack of settled determination.
When the disturbance of <s>dharma</s> and the breaking of that [established order occurs], how are <s>śūdras</s> and the rest competent?
And if [one says] that when [the teaching] is imparted by the three upper <s>varṇas</s>, another [i.e., a <s>śūdra</s>] too may trust [it]—
this itself demonstrates his lack of qualification for the investigation of logic.
Where there is perpetual independence from the <s>Vedas</s> in perception and inference,
there, as stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> with "except for the <s>śūdra</s>," even the <s>śūdra</s> and others may be qualified.
The <s>Bhagavān</s> spoke of the fourteen branches of <s>dharma</s> and knowledge
as not to be touched by <s>śūdras</s>, in the <s>Āśvamedhika</s> [<s>parvan</s>]:
"The <s>Aṅgas</s> (auxiliary sciences), the four <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, the elaboration of logic (<s>Nyāyavistara</s>),
the <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>—these are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
These branches of knowledge that have been properly declared by me, O <s>Bhārata</s>,
have arisen as purifying [instruments] and indeed for the purpose of purification.
Therefore these should not be touched by a <s>śūdra</s> in any way."
Thus [ends the quotation].

children.text:
tasmādetāni traivarṇikairadhyetavyāni /
tatra brāhmaṇena vidyāprāptaye dharmānuṣṭhānāya cādhigantavyāni /
kṣatriyavaiśyābhyāṃ dharmānuṣṭhānāyaiva /

children.translated_text: Similarly, <s>Śaṅkha</s>, having enumerated the branches of knowledge, has stated: "These a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is qualified [to study].
And he demonstrates the procedure for the others."
This has been established in exactly the same way by the compilers of <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>.

children.text: tataśca yeṣāṃ karmabrahmamīmāṃsāvaseyatattvahitarūpaprameyacintādhikāraḥ, teṣāmeva tātparyaparyavasāyitayā dharmavidyāsthānābhimatanyāyaṃvistarāndhikārapa iti siddham //
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is established that those who have the qualification for the inquiry into the true nature of reality that is to be ascertained through <s>Karma-Mīmāṃsā</s> and <s>Brahma-Mīmāṃsā</s> and that constitutes the beneficial object of knowledge—they alone, as those in whom the ultimate purport comes to rest, have the qualification for the elaboration of logic that is regarded as a branch of the knowledge of <s>dharma</s>.

Therefore these [fourteen branches] are to be studied by the three upper <s>varṇas</s>.
Among them, by a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> they are to be mastered for the attainment of knowledge and for the practice of <s>dharma</s>.
By the <s>kṣatriya</s> and <s>vaiśya</s>, only for the practice of <s>dharma</s>.
<s>Nyā</s>. <s>Pa</s>. <s>Pra</s>. 5.
Determination of the purpose.
By means of <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge) such as <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and the rest, there is the purification of words and their meanings;
the determination of the relation between <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) and <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge) and so on; and the authoritativeness of what is stated in the directives.
In cases like the injunction "let one navigate with stones" and the like, the alternative meaning [is established] on the basis of contradiction;
in cases like the <s>Citrā</s> full-moon sacrifice, the non-animality of the victim, and the nature of the result, the resolution [is achieved] through the avenue of non-sublation.
The deliberation on <s>anuvāda</s> (restatement), <s>vidhāna</s> (injunction), and the like is preceded by [considerations of] entailment and so forth;
when perception and the rest are not established, [such deliberation] cannot be devised in any way.
With such and similar uses, the elaboration of logic was declared by the sages
as a branch of the knowledge of <s>dharma</s>, because it supports the <s>Vedas</s>.
When the <s>pramāṇa</s> called <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony) has been purified through the elaboration of logic,
<s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, [dealing with] its specific [applications], would establish the authoritativeness [of scripture] regarding <s>dharma</s>.
And the purification of the object of knowledge [comes] ultimately from the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>;
the inclusion of that [inquiry] here, however, is for establishing its purposive connection and the like.

children.text:
pramāṇamevāsya śāstrasya prādhānyato viṣayaḥ /
tatra prekṣāvadadhicikīrṣāsiddhyartham---prameyatattvajñānaṃ hānopādānadvārā niḥśreyasahetuḥ, tacca saparikarāt pramāṇāt---iti paramparayā prayojanajñāpanāya pradarśanamātramihābhimatam /
ataḥ pradhānaviṣayatayā, prameyādisādhakatayā ca pramāṇaṃ prameyādapi pūrvamucyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>pramāṇa</s> is discussed before <s>prameya</s> and the rest, both as the primary subject matter and as the means of establishing <s>prameya</s> and the rest.

children.text: tatra vyavacchedyatvāṅgatvādimukhena saṃśayādayo 'pi caturdaśa yathāyathaṃ nirūpyante /
children.translated_text: Therein, <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) and the other [categories], all fourteen, are also examined in their respective places, through aspects such as being that which is to be excluded and being auxiliary [to the main inquiry].

children.text: na ca ṣoḍaśatve nirbandhaḥ, atathātvaviparyayatvādyupādhyantarādhīnasaṃgrahavibhajanābhyāṃ nyūnādhikoddeśasyāpi śakyatvāt upayogānupayogāviśeṣācca /
children.translated_text: Nor is there insistence on [exactly] sixteen [categories], since by different classificatory principles such as "not being so" and "being the contrary" and the like, both fewer and more items in the enumeration are possible through [different modes of] inclusion and division, and since there is no difference in utility.
This alone is also the intention of <s>Gautama</s> himself.

The primary subject of this <s>śāstra</s> is <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) itself.
Regarding that, for the accomplishment of what a discerning person wishes to undertake—knowledge of the true nature of the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is the cause of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) through the avenues of avoidance and adoption; and that [knowledge arises] from <s>pramāṇa</s> together with its auxiliaries—thus, what is intended here is merely an indication for making known the purpose through a chain of connections.
<s>Nyā</s>. <s>Pa</s>. <s>Pra</s>. 6.
Establishment of the distinction between <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) and <s>apramāṇa</s> (invalid means of knowledge).
To begin with, there is this well-known highway of the discourse of worldly examiners: "this is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, this is an <s>apramāṇa</s>."
But if that [distinction] is disregarded, then examination itself cannot arise, for lack of any basis.
For the practical activity of the world operates on the basis of something;

children.text: na tatsāmānyato nāsti kathantā tu parīkṣyate //
children.translated_text: it is not the case that such [basis] does not exist in general; only the specific details are to be examined.
When the general [nature of knowledge] has been ascertained, and a particular [case] is desired to be investigated,
examination is appropriate, [and it] consists in generating the <s>pramāṇa</s> that one accepts.
Not everything is invalid as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, for [that claim would entail] the destruction of one's own position by itself;
nor is everything valid as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, for [that claim would entail] the destruction of one's own position by others.
The establishment and non-establishment of one's own position—this is a settled fact of common experience;
but from the establishment or non-establishment of that [common experience], your position [that everything is valid or invalid] can never be established.
The sublation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is refuted because it is self-contradictory;

children.text: apramāṇena tadbādhe sādhanaṃ ca tato na kim //
children.translated_text: if sublation of it [is attempted] by a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>, then why is that [non-<s>pramāṇa</s>] not also a means of proof [and hence a <s>pramāṇa</s>]?
If the establishment of [valid] knowledge does not come from a non-<s>pramāṇa</s> or from a <s>pramāṇa</s>—that is not so,
because the establishment of it [comes] from a <s>pramāṇa</s>, which protects both itself and the other [i.e., the object known].
The determination of sublation and non-sublation also comes from [valid] knowledge, not from something unsettled;
otherwise, from the unsettledness [itself], there can be no determination—this is established.
If nothing at all is determined, there can be neither the arising of doubt nor any determination;
just as one alternative of that [doubt] is established, so too is it possible with respect to other [cases].
When the alternatives, which have a form common to the subject (<s>dharmin</s>), have been previously determined,
the doubt "is this one such, or is this one such?" arises.
Doubt does not exist everywhere—this too is seen by everyone;
"everything is doubtful"—do you, the clever one, have certainty about this?
And [your] doubt is not itself doubtful, O proponent of doubtful non-duality!
Even having gone far [in argument], the determination in your doubt is inescapable.
Therefore, when the division between <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>apramāṇa</s> has been established in general,
a definition (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) is set forth for the removal of occasional doubt.

children.text: tatra vyutpattivivakṣābhedāt pramitiṃ tatkaraṇaṃ ca yathecchaṃ pramāṇamāhurityavocāma, āśrayaprāmāṇyasyānādeśikatvāt /
children.translated_text: There, due to differences in etymological derivation and intended meaning, we have already stated that <s>pramāṇa</s> may refer to <s>pramiti</s> (valid cognition) or to its instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), as one chooses, since the authoritativeness of the [cognition's] locus has not been prescribed [as fixed].
"From the authoritativeness of the trustworthy (<s>āpta</s>)"—the meaning is: authoritativeness [of testimony arises] from the cause of having been spoken by a trustworthy person.

children.text: na hi vaktṛprāmāṇyaṃ vākyaprāmāṇya upayujyate laukikavākyeṣu; kintu kāraṇadoṣābhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the authoritativeness of the speaker is not what is relevant to the authoritativeness of a sentence in ordinary [non-scriptural] sentences; rather, [what is relevant is] the absence of defect in the cause.
In both senses [of <s>pramāṇa</s>], it is <s>pramiti</s> (valid cognition) itself that is to be examined.
<s>Nyā</s>. <s>Pa</s>. <s>Pra</s>. 7.
Examination of the definition of <s>pramā</s> (valid cognition).

children.text: tatrāsmadīyā eva kecidanyathākhyātimicchantaḥ smṛteḥ prāmāṇyamanicchantaḥ samyaganubhavaḥ prameti lakṣayanti; ubhayamicchantaḥ, yathārthajñānaṃ prameti; ubhayamanicchantaḥ, anubhūtiḥ prameti /
children.translated_text: Among our own [<s>Viśiṣṭādvaita</s>] thinkers, some, who accept <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (apprehension-as-otherwise) [as the theory of error] and do not accept the authoritativeness of <s>smṛti</s> (memory), define <s>pramā</s> as "a correct experience" (<s>samyag anubhava</s>); those who accept both [<s>anyathākhyāti</s> and the authoritativeness of <s>smṛti</s>] define it as "knowledge of a thing as it is" (<s>yathārtha-jñāna</s>); and those who accept neither define it as "experience" (<s>anubhūti</s>) [itself].
And definitions of similar kinds have been stated by other disputants as well.

children.text: vayaṃ tu brūmaḥ--- yathāvasthitavyavahārānuguṇaṃ jñānaṃ prameti /
children.translated_text: We, however, say: <s>pramā</s> is cognition that is conducive to activity conforming to the actual state of affairs (<s>yathāvasthita-vyavahāra</s>).
Whether one accepts <s>yathārthakhyāti</s> (apprehension-as-it-is), <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension), or indeed <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (apprehension-as-otherwise),
this [definition] should not be disputed, since it follows common experience.
That the mere fact of being <s>smṛti</s> (memory) constitutes invalidity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>—this is not proper, as will be explained,
because in common experience, an unsublated <s>smṛti</s> is accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And in the rejection of Buddhist scripture and the like, the fact of being rooted in <s>smṛti</s> is not the reason [for rejection].
For then the same consequence would apply even to the <s>Mānavadharmaśāstra</s> and the rest, which are also rooted in pure <s>smṛti</s>.

children.text: bhrāntiṃ pramāto bhindanto na cāhuḥ smṛtimānatām /
children.translated_text: And those who distinguish error from valid cognition do not assert the validity of <s>smṛti</s> [as such];
for, in your view, the mere fact of being <s>smṛti</s> is clearly [what constitutes] invalidity.
And in cases like the erroneous perception of a conch-shell as yellow, this [position] is not tenable;

children.text: cakṣuṣaiva hi śaṅkhādeḥ pītimādeśca tatra dhīḥ //
children.translated_text: for the cognition of yellowness and so forth regarding the conch-shell and the rest is indeed [produced] by the visual organ alone.
Therefore, whether in the [initial] cognition or in the arising of [subsequent] practical activity,
the determination of valid cognition and error is [to be made] through the [cognition's] conformity or non-conformity [to the actual state of affairs].
The exclusion of <s>viparyaya</s> (error) and the rest is established in exactly this way;
for any cognition that involves "otherness" [from what is actually the case] is regarded as erroneous.
Even in the doctrines of <s>ātmakhyāti</s> (self-apprehension) and the rest, [this element of] otherness is not precluded;
for the erroneous activity, sublation, and the rest cannot be [explained] otherwise.
This being so, the cognition that apprehends otherwise, or else its causal complex, on grounds of parsimony,
remains as the cause of activity not conforming to reality.
<s>Anyathākhyāti</s> (apprehension-as-otherwise) is the most parsimonious [theory], being impossible to abandon by all [theorists];
since even the proponent of that [rival] theory cannot avoid it, <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension) is [claimed to be] even more parsimonious than that.
Natural suitability lies with <s>anyathākhyāti</s>, while parsimony is established for <s>akhyāti</s>—
in order to show this, both [theories] are left unrejected in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [of <s>Rāmānuja</s>].
What <s>Nāthamuni</s>, <s>Miśra</s> (i.e., <s>Yāmuna</s>), and others [established as] the proof of <s>yathārthakhyāti</s> (apprehension-as-it-is),
some have called an [expression of] exuberant elaboration, since it does not mount upon the understanding of common people.
Even if silver and the like exist [in the shell] on the basis of a <s>pramāṇa</s>, one of the two [aspects] is certain:
either the incapacity to produce the [expected] effect is not apprehended, or the capacity to produce [that effect] is apprehended [instead].
The defects of the other <s>khyāti</s> (error) theories, however, become manifest of their own accord when one studies the respective doctrines;
therefore, [only] a little is said here by way of summary.

children.text: tatrātmakhyātau tāvat--- anyadvijñānamastīti dhīranyaviṣayā na vā /
children.translated_text: First, regarding <s>ātmakhyāti</s> (the theory that error is the apprehension of cognition itself as an object): is the cognition that "another cognition exists" a cognition that has another [i.e., external] object, or not?
In the first case, even of that [external] object there would be a cognition of the same kind, and [ultimately] there would be only one cognition [directed] elsewhere [than itself].
The cognition in another [momentary] continuum, or [a cognition] at another moment in one's own continuum—

children.text: yā dhīḥ sādhayate sā hi svato bāhyaṃ vigāhate //
children.translated_text: the cognition that establishes that, of its own nature, apprehends what is external.
The invariable rule of co-perception [of object and cognition], and the fact that being apprehended is a mark of cognition—
[these do not prove that] in cognition too the object is [merely] "as if"; thus the identity of cognition and object would not [be established] thereby.
Even if the network of causes such as defects and the like is accepted as illusory [by the Yogācāra],
and even if the substratum is also illusory, error is equally unavoidable.
Therefore, in that case, only the position of the <s>Mādhyamika</s> remains;
and there is no escape even there, since [the position] is untenable in every way.
Do you assert the non-existence [of things] in the conventional sense, or in the ultimate sense?
In the former case, the negation is not unqualified—[conventional existence] is no different [from what is real], and [conventional existence] is not something that is not a basis for cognition.

children.text: catuṣkoṭivimuktaṃ ca tattvaṃ prāmāṇikaṃ na vā /
children.translated_text: And is the reality that is free from the four alternatives (<s>catuṣkoṭi</s>) established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> or not?

children.text: pūrvatra tāvatī sattā na cet taddhīrasanmatiḥ //
children.translated_text: In the former case, it has that much reality; if not, the cognition of it is a false cognition.

children.text: anyeṣāṃ ca niradhiṣṭhānakhyātau --- atrāsadeva bhavatāmatreti khyāyate na vā /
children.translated_text: And regarding the <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension) of others, [which holds that error has] no [real] substratum: is what appears here as "this" for you actually unreal, or not?
In the first case, a substratum is [already] established; in the second case, [there is] a denial of [the very] appearance.
Moreover, the <s>timira</s> (eye-disease) situated in one's own eye, by those afflicted with <s>timira</s>,
appears thus due to its resemblance to a cluster of hairs — such cases are of this kind. //
Even though a non-existent object may appear as if existent,
nevertheless, that [appearance] is not the substratum — for it is limited to its own location and so forth. //
Others understand superimposition upon the object cognized as 'this' through the cognition of 'this-ness';
and the superimposition of 'this-ness' upon that [substratum] — in terms of result, the two are equivalent. //

children.text: anirvacanīyakhyātau --- anirvācyatayā vastu nirucyeta na vā tvayā /
children.translated_text: On the <s>anirvācanīya-khyāti</s> (theory of indescribable error) --- Would you or would you not express a thing as <s>anirvācya</s> (indescribable)?
In the first case, there are manifold contradictions; in the second, our own doctrine stands firm. //
If the exclusion from both being and non-being is apprehended as contradictory,

children.text: sadasadrūpatā kiṃ nu pratītā tu na gṛhyate //
children.translated_text: then why is the nature of being both real and unreal, which is indeed experienced, not apprehended? //
Like what is neither hot nor cold, the difference from <s>tuccha</s> (absolute void) and from <s>Brahman</s>
would have to be established; if that is already established through the sublation of the error-theory and so forth, then that is [already] our [position]. //
Nor does the sublation of the entire [world] arise of its own accord;
and through reasoning that is itself unestablished, such sublation would touch even <s>Brahman</s> itself. //
If otherness from the real is admitted at the time of destruction because of destruction,
and if sublation were to occur at its own time [of existence], then even destruction would be inexplicable. //

children.text: nityatvena śrutānāṃ ca keṣāṃ cinna hi nāśitā /
children.translated_text: And of certain things declared as eternal by <s>śruti</s> (scripture), there is no destruction at all;
hence the reason [for anirvācanīyatva] fails in part, and there is no identity between destruction and sublation. //
On the <s>nirviṣaya-khyāti</s> (theory of objectless error) --- The adoption of another theory of error on account of the unreality of the object, etc.,
and the [claim of] non-apprehension — the cognition of silver and the like — has been refuted by the argument [already given]. //
<s>Nyā. Pa. Pra.</s> 8 //
Conclusion //
Therefore, in this matter, either erroneous cognition or cognition of something possessing that cause —
error is the cause of the practical activity regarding an object whose [true] nature is different. //

children.text: iti śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau pratyakṣādhyāye prathamamāhnikam //
children.translated_text: Thus concludes the first <s>āhnika</s> (session) in the chapter on <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) in the <s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, among the works of the blessed <s>Veṅkaṭanātha</s>, <s>Vedāntācārya</s>, the lion among poets and logicians, master of all systems. //
// Salutation to the blessed <s>Nigamānta Mahādeśika</s>! //
<s>Nyā. Pa. Pra.</s> 9 //
The second <s>āhnika</s> (session). //

children.text: tadihānyathākhyātipakṣe viparyayasya saṃśayasya ca vyavacchedārtham "yathāvasthitavyavahārānuguṇaṃ jñānam" iti pramāṇalakṣaṇe yathāvasthitādiviśeṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: Here, in the <s>anyathā-khyāti</s> (theory of error as misapprehension) position, for the purpose of distinguishing <s>viparyaya</s> (misapprehension) and <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt), the qualifier 'yathāvasthita' (as things actually are) and so on in the definition of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge) as 'cognition that accords with the actual state of affairs for practical activity.'
Even in the <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension) position, cognition that has not entered into the totality [of valid cognition] is designated by the word 'that' [in the definition];
and that cognition is <s>apramāṇa</s> (invalid knowledge) in that context — since this is well-established in common experience, it is indeed something to be excluded.
Even there, the veridicality of each individual component is not impaired. //
<s>Nyā. Pa. Pra.</s> 10 //
Examination of <s>viparyaya</s> (misapprehension). //
In the first position [<s>anyathā-khyāti</s>], <s>viparyaya</s> is the determination of one thing as another.

children.text: dvitīye tu pakṣe sāmānyato dharmisphuraṇe sati apratipannatadvirodhaviruddhaviśeṣādhyavasāya iti //
children.translated_text: In the second position [<s>akhyāti</s>], however, when there is a manifestation of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) in general terms, it is the determination of a particular that is contradictory to the unapprehended [actual particular] that contradicts it. //

children.text:
sa cāyamanekavidhaḥ---ekānekaviruddhaviśeṣasphuraṇāt /
tatra ekaviśeṣasphuraṇaṃ yathā--- pītaḥ śaṅkha ityādi /
anekaviśeṣasphuraṇaṃ yathā---ekameva bhinnamabhinnaṃ cetyādyanekāntavādinām, prapañcaḥ sadvilakṣaṇo 'sadvilakṣaṇaścetyādyadvaitavādinām /
parasparaviruddhānekaviśeṣavatar idṛśasya viparyayasya saṃśayādbhedo mithovirodhābhimānaviraheṇa samuccitādhyavasāyaḥ /
dharmavirodhe parasparāviruddhānekaviśeṣasphuraṇaṃ yathā--- vipulatvaikatvaviśiṣṭe candre alpatvadvitvādigrahaḥ /
viparyayameva dharmāntaradharmyantarabhedādanyathākhyātiviparītakhyātibhedena kvacidvyavaharanti /
yathā pītaśaṅkharajjusarpabhramau /

children.translated_text: And <s>rajas</s> (passion) and <s>tamas</s> (darkness) are proclaimed to be the root of these two —
"That intellect by which one wrongly understands <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) and <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness), what ought to be done and what ought not to be done —
that intellect, O <s>Pārtha</s>, is <s>rājasī</s> (of the nature of passion). //

And this [<s>viparyaya</s>] is of many kinds — due to the manifestation of one, many, or mutually contradictory particulars. Among these, the manifestation of a single [wrong] particular is illustrated by: 'the conch is yellow,' and so forth. The manifestation of many [wrong] particulars is illustrated by: the <s>Anekāntavādins</s> (Jains) [who hold] 'the one thing is both different and non-different,' and the <s>Advaitavādins</s> [who hold] 'the world is different from the real and different from the unreal,' and so forth. The distinction between such <s>viparyaya</s> involving mutually contradictory multiple particulars and <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) is that [in <s>viparyaya</s>] there is a combined determination without awareness of the mutual contradiction. When there is contradiction among properties, the manifestation of multiple particulars that are not mutually contradictory is illustrated by: in the case of the moon, which possesses the particulars of largeness and singularity, the apprehension of smallness, duality, and so forth. Some classify <s>viparyaya</s> itself into <s>anyathā-khyāti</s> (misapprehension of properties) and <s>viparīta-khyāti</s> (misapprehension of the substratum), based on the distinction of different properties versus different substrata. For example, the errors of a yellow conch and a rope-snake [respectively].

children.text: adharmaṃ dharmamiti yā manyate tamasā vṛtā /
children.translated_text: That which, enveloped by <s>tamas</s> (darkness), regards <s>adharma</s> as <s>dharma</s>,
and all things in a perverted manner — that intellect, O <s>Pārtha</s>, is <s>tāmasī</s> (of the nature of darkness)." //
Thus.

children.text:
yadyapi rajjusarpādibhrame rajjutvādidharmaviparītasarpatvādidharmādhyāsa eva, tathāpi svarūpanirūpakadharmatvenāntaraṅgatayā dharmivaiparītyavyapadeśaḥ /
śvaityādestu nirūpitasvarūpaviśeṣakatvameva /
vivaraṇe tvevamuktam--- "trividhamajñānam---svarūpājñānam, anyathājñānam,viparītajñānamiti /

children.translated_text: <s>Svarūpa-ajñāna</s> (ignorance of the essential nature) is the non-apprehension of a thing.

children.text: anyathājñānaṃ vastuno vastvantaratayā bhānam; yathā---śukteḥ rūpyatayā /
children.translated_text: <s>Anyathā-jñāna</s> (cognition as other) is the appearance of a thing as something else; for example, the appearance of mother-of-pearl as silver.

children.text: viparītajñānaṃ tu yathāvat vastuni bhāsamāne yuktibhistasyānyathopapādanam; yathā---jñātṛtayā ahantvena ātmani bhāsamāne 'pi kuyuktibhirasyabhrāntitopapādanaṃ kudṛśām" iti /
children.translated_text: <s>Viparīta-jñāna</s> (contrary cognition), however, is when a thing appears as it actually is, yet through reasoning one construes it otherwise; for example, even though the self appears in its nature as a knower, as possessing 'I-ness,' the wrong reasoners' establishment through fallacious arguments that this is not error." Thus.

The arising of <s>viparyaya</s> occurs, as appropriate, through <s>adharma</s> (demerit), defects of the sense organs, fallacious reasoning, habitual practice, faulty induction, deceptive utterances, and similar factors, assisted by non-apprehension of the truth. //

Although in errors such as the rope-snake, there is indeed a superimposition of properties like serpent-hood which are contrary to the actual properties like rope-hood, nevertheless, the designation as 'misapprehension of the substratum' is made because [the superimposed property] is more intimately related as a property that defines the essential nature. Whereas whiteness and the like are merely qualifiers of an already determined essence. But in the <s>Vivaraṇa</s>, it is stated thus: "<s>Ajñāna</s> (ignorance) is threefold: <s>svarūpa-ajñāna</s> (ignorance of the essential nature), <s>anyathā-jñāna</s> (cognition as other than what it is), and <s>viparīta-jñāna</s> (contrary cognition).
<s>Nyā. Pa. Pra.</s> 11 //
Examination of <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt). //

children.text:
sāmānyadharmisphuraṇe sati apratipannatadvirodhapratipannamithovirodhānekaviśeṣasphuraṇaṃ saṃśayaḥ /
yathā---ūrdhvavastumātragrahaṇe sati tadvirodhitayānanusaṃdhīyamānayormithaḥsphuṭavirodhayoḥ sthāṇutvapuruṣatvayoḥ sphuraṇam---ayaṃ sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti /
mitho virodhāgrahaṇe tayorvikalpo na syāt /
tata eva "ḍolāvegavadatra sphuraṇakramaḥ" ityeke, ekasmin yugapadanyonyapratikṣepasya dhīviruddhatvāt /
atra "caitanyasya viṣayeṇa dṛḍhasaṃyogo hi niścayaḥ /
tasyaiva bahubhiryugapadadṛḍhasaṃyogaḥ saṃśayaḥ" ityātmasiddhigrantho 'pi na viruddhaḥ; itarathā jñānārthayordṛḍhādṛḍhasaṃśleṣanirūpaṇānupapatteḥ /
yugapaditi tu śaighṣamātraparam /
yaugapadyābhyupagame 'pi adṛḍhatvaṃ parasparapratikṣepaprakāraviśeṣa eva; anyathā ayamūrdhvo vā sthāṇurvetyādisaṃśayaprasaṅgaḥ /
yadyapyaviruddheṣvapi keṣucidadharmādimūlakavirodhagrahaṇāt keṣāñcidīdṛśo 'pi saṃśayaḥ saṃbhavati; yathā--- ātmā jñānaṃ vā jñātā veti, jñānaṃ dharmo dharmi vetyādi; tathāpyābhimānikaṃ parasparapratikṣepitvaṃ tatrāpyastyeva /
asya ca samānadharmavipratipattibhyāmevāsādhāraṇakāraṇābhyāmadharmādisahitābhyāṃ yathāsaṃbhavamudbhavaḥ /
taduktaṃ tattvaratnākare--- "kaścaiṣa saṃśayaḥ katividhaśca? ekasmin dharmiṇi viruddhānekaviśeṣāvabhāsaḥ saṃśayaḥ /
sa ca dvividhaḥ---" ityādinā /
tatra samānadharmaḥ sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ /
tajjanito yathā---ūrdhvatvāviśeṣāt sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti /
agṛhyamāṇabalatāratamyaviruddhānekajñāpakopasthāpanamiha vipratipattiḥ /
sā ca sajātīyavijātīyābhāsarūpadvitricaturādijñāpakabhedādbahuprakārā /
pratyakṣatadābhāsavipratipatteḥ saṃśayo yathā--- cakṣuṣā samukhaṃ pratibhāti darpaṇatalam, sparśanena tvanyathā; kimidaṃ samukhaṃ nirmukhaṃ veti /
anumānatadābhāsavipratipatteryathā--- dhūmavattvāt parvato 'gnimān, nirālokatvādanagnirityatra sāgniranagnirveti /
śrutivipratipatteryathā---bhedābhedavyapadeśābhyāṃ jīvo brahmaṇo bhinno 'bhinno vetyādi /
vādivipratipatteryathā---vaiśeṣikaupaniṣadavākyadvayaśrāviṇo madhyasthabuddheḥ kimindriyāṇi bhautikāni, āhaṅkārikāṇi veti /
evaṃ pāmarādivākyavipratipatterapi ---nadyāstīre phalāni santi, na santi vetyādi /
children.translated_text: Similarly, from conflicting testimony even of ordinary persons and the like — 'There are fruits on the riverbank' versus 'There are not' — and so forth.

children.text: pratyakṣānumānavipratipatteryathā---cakṣuṣā pītaśaṅkhabhrame śaṅkhatvācca sitatvānumāne, kimayaṃ śaṅkhaḥ pītaḥ sito veti /
children.translated_text: Doubt from conflict between perception and inference is illustrated by: in the error of perceiving a yellow conch, combined with the inference of whiteness from its being a conch — 'Is this conch yellow or white?'

Doubt from conflict between perception and scripture is illustrated by: 'Am I a [gross] object, large, or atomic?' [i.e., perception shows a large body, while scripture teaches the atomic nature of the self].

children.text: anumānāgamavipratipatteryathā --- kiṃ paramāṇūpādānaṃ jagat, uta brahmopādānamiti eṣā dik //
children.translated_text: Doubt from conflict between inference and scripture is illustrated by: 'Is the world produced from atoms, or is it produced from <s>Brahman</s>?' — this is the general direction. //

When there is a manifestation of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) in general terms, <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) is the manifestation of multiple particulars whose mutual contradiction has been apprehended but which are not recognized as contradicting [the unapprehended actual particular]. For example — when there is mere apprehension of an upright object, and when the two [alternatives] — being a post and being a person — whose contradiction with each other has been clearly recognized, are not ascertained as contradicting that [object], their manifestation occurs: 'Is this a post or a person?' Without the apprehension of the mutual contradiction between the two, there would be no alternation between them. From this very consideration, some say 'the order of manifestation here is like the swinging of a pendulum,' since the simultaneous mutual exclusion of the two in a single [cognition] would contradict cognition. Here, the statement in the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s> text — 'A firm connection of consciousness with the object is <s>niścaya</s> (certainty); an unfirm connection of the same [consciousness] with many [objects] simultaneously is <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt)' — is also not contradicted; for otherwise, the explanation of firm and unfirm connection between cognition and object would be impossible. The word 'simultaneously' refers merely to rapidity. Even if simultaneity is accepted, the unfirmness consists precisely in the specific mode of mutual exclusion; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of doubt such as 'Is this upright, or is it a post?' Although even regarding non-contradictory things, some may have such doubt due to apprehension of contradiction rooted in <s>adharma</s> (demerit) and such — for example, 'Is the self knowledge or is it the knower?', 'Is knowledge a property or a substance?', and so forth — nevertheless, even there, a notional mutual exclusion indeed exists. And the arising of this [doubt] is from the two uncommon causes alone, namely, the perception of a common property and conflicting testimony, assisted by <s>adharma</s> and the like, as appropriate. Thus it is stated in the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>: 'What is this doubt, and of how many kinds? Doubt is the appearance of mutually contradictory multiple particulars in a single <s>dharmin</s> (substratum). And it is of two kinds —' and so on. There, 'common property' means a property that is shared [by both alternatives]. That which arises from it is illustrated by: 'Is it a post or a person?' due to the non-distinction of uprightness [which is common to both]. <s>Vipratipatti</s> (conflicting testimony) here means the presentation of multiple indicators that reveal mutually contradictory things, whose relative strength is not apprehended. And this is of many varieties, owing to the distinction among two, three, four, or more indicators that may be homogeneous or heterogeneous. Doubt arising from conflict between perception and its semblance is illustrated by: a mirror surface appears face-on to the eye, but otherwise to touch — 'Is this face-on or not?' Doubt from conflict between inference and its semblance is illustrated by: 'The mountain has fire because of smoke; it has no fire because of absence of light' — 'Does it have fire or not?' Doubt from conflicting scriptural testimony is illustrated by: from statements of both difference and non-difference, 'Is the <s>jīva</s> (individual self) different from or non-different from <s>Brahman</s>?' and so forth. Doubt from conflicting doctrinal testimony is illustrated by: in the mind of a neutral person who has heard both the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> and <s>Aupaniṣada</s> statements — 'Are the sense organs material (<s>bhautika</s>) or derived from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego)?'

children.text: kecittu vipratipattiśabdamātre muhyanto vādivipratipattimeva vipratipattiṃ manyante, tadayuktam, viśeṣābhāvāt //
children.translated_text: But some, confused merely by the word '<s>vipratipatti</s>' (conflicting testimony), think that only doctrinal disagreement among disputants constitutes <s>vipratipatti</s>; this is incorrect, because there is no [basis for such] distinction. //
What is stated in the <s>Prajñāparitrāṇa</s>: 'From seeing a common form, from apprehending multiple appearances,
and from the dispute of the learned — doubt is accepted as threefold.' //

children.text: iti ; tadapi nūnaṃ parānukāramātram, dvitīyatṛtīyayorakairāśyāt grāhakāvāntarabhedasyātiprasaṅgitvāt aprayojakatvācca /
children.translated_text: That too is surely mere imitation of others, since the second and third [causes] cannot be separated [from each other], since the sub-distinction among apprehenders [in the second] would lead to over-extension, and since [the distinction] serves no purpose.

children.text: atra cānekākāragraho nānākāragraho vivakṣitaḥ, na tvanekavyāvṛttāsādhāraṇākāragrahaḥ, anantaram "artheṣveṣvaviśeṣeṇa dvyākāragrāhidhīdvayam /
children.translated_text: And here, 'apprehension of multiple appearances' is intended as apprehension of diverse appearances, not apprehension of an uncommon appearance excluded from many; for immediately after, with the words 'two cognitions apprehending two appearances without distinction among these objects —'
and so on, that very [interpretation] is illustrated. //

children.text:
asādhāraṇadharmādapi kecit saṃśayamāhuḥ; yathā---gandhavattvāt pṛthivī nityā anityā vetyādi /
atra gandhavattvasya nityātmādivyāvṛtteḥ kṛtakatvādivadanityatvasmārakatvam, anityābādivyāvṛtterniravayavatvādivannityatvasmārakatvamiti viruddhaviśeṣadvayānvitasamānadharmasyeva tadubhayavyāvṛttāsādhāraṇadharmasyāpi saṃśayahetutvamupapannamiti, tadayuktam; na hi tatra gandhavattvādinā saṃśayotpattiḥ, api tu vyatirekanirūpaṇavilambāprāgeva gandhādiviśiṣṭadravyasya nityānityasādhāraṇatayā bhāsamānairdravyatvādibhireva /
tatrānyataraśironirṇinīṣayā viśeṣakadharmacintāyāṃ tu gandhavattvamubhayānanvitatvādubhayorapyaniṣkarṣamityetāvadeva cintyate /
kevalavyatirekibhaṅge caitadviśadaṃ bhaviṣyati /
gandhavattvāt pṛthivī nityā vā anityā veti tu yadā kaścidvyavaharet, tatrāpi gandhavattvaṃ nityatvānityatvayoranyatarasya prayojakaṃ na vā ityeva saṃdehaḥ /

children.translated_text: And even that [doubt] is from common properties alone, characterized by property-hood and such.

children.text: atha nityavyāvṛttadharmavattvādanityatvam anityavyāvṛttadharmavattvācca nityatvaṃ puraskṛtya nityā anityā veti saṃśate; tadāpi hetubhūtadharmadvayanimitto 'yaṃ saṃśayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, if one doubts 'is it eternal or non-eternal?' on the basis that it possesses a property that excludes the eternal and hence is non-eternal, and possesses a property that excludes the non-eternal and hence is eternal — even then, this doubt is occasioned by two properties serving as reasons.
For here there is certainly not a single reason.

children.text: gandhastu tatra sāmānyarūpastaṭasthaḥ; na tu hetuḥ //
children.translated_text: Smell, in that context, is merely an incidental accompaniment in a general role; it is not the cause [of doubt]. //

Some also assert doubt from an uncommon property; for example, 'Earth, possessing smell, is eternal or non-eternal?' Here, since smell-possession excludes [earth] from eternal things like the self and so forth, it can remind one of non-eternality like the property of being produced; and since it excludes [earth] from non-eternal things like atoms and so forth, it can remind one of eternality like the property of being partless — thus, just as a common property associated with two contradictory particulars [can cause doubt], so too an uncommon property excluded from both can be a cause of doubt. But this is incorrect; for there, doubt does not arise from smell-possession and such, but rather, even before the delay of examining the negative concomitance, from properties like substance-hood itself, which appear as common to both eternal and non-eternal substances qualified by smell and so forth. When, in the investigation of the distinguishing property with the desire to determine one or the other alternative, smell-possession is not associated with either — only this much is being considered: that it fails to yield a conclusion for either. And this will become clear in the section on the refutation of purely negative inference (<s>kevala-vyatirekin</s>). When someone says 'Earth, because of possessing smell, is eternal or non-eternal,' even there, the doubt is merely whether smell-possession is productive of one or the other, or not at all.
Some also subsume <s>vipratipatti</s> (conflicting testimony) under common property alone.

children.text: yathā hi ūrdhvatvamubhayasādhāraṇam, tathā vādiparigṛhītatvāderapi sādhāraṇatvāt vimativiṣayasya dharmiṇo vā sāmānyaveṣasya tadubhayasādhāraṇyāditi /
children.translated_text: Just as uprightness is common to both [post and person], so too, since the property of being accepted by a disputant and the like is common [to both alternatives], or since the generality-form of the <s>dharmin</s> (substratum) that is the subject of dispute is common to both — thus [they argue].

Even so, just as common property has the capacity to remind one of post-hood and person-hood [previously] experienced together [with that common property], so too <s>vipratipatti</s> (conflicting testimony), being an independent reminder of specific [alternatives] without depending on the inferential process from common property, and being prior to it [in operation] and relied upon by it, directly establishes the capacity to remind one of those specific [alternatives] — hence the twofold division has been stated by us. //

children.text:
punaścāyaṃ dvitricaturādiśirodhikaraṇabhedādbahuvidhaḥ; yathā--- ayaṃ sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti, ghaṭaḥ satyo 'satyo nirvacanīyo 'nirvacanīyo vetyādi /
tathā imau sthāṇū vā puruṣau vā, ete padārthāḥ satyā asatyā nirvacanīyā anirvacanīyā vetyādi /
yastu dvayoranyatarasya coratve siddhe ayaṃ coraḥ ayaṃ vā cora iti saṃdehaḥ, sa tu ayaṃ coro na vā ityevaṃrūpasaṃśayadvayasamāhāraḥ /
yadvā yaścoraḥ, saḥ ayam ayaṃ vā ityeka eva /
children.translated_text: Or alternatively, it is a single [doubt]: 'The one who is the thief — is he this one or that one?'
Or again: 'Does the thief-hood belong to this one, or to that one?'

children.text: yadyapyubhayavyatiriktapuruṣacoratvābhāvo tayoranyatarasya coratve vā tātparyānnirṇayagarbhatvam, tathāpi ubhayoranyataraviśeṣanirṇayābhāvāt tasminnaṃśe saṃśaya eva /
children.translated_text: Although the absence of thief-hood in anyone other than the two, or the certainty that one of the two is the thief — due to its purport — implies that [the doubt] is pregnant with a determination, nevertheless, since there is no determination of which specific one of the two [is the thief], in that respect it is indeed doubt.

children.text: na caikasyāpi jñānasya saṃśayanirṇayātmatāvirodhaḥ, sarvasminnapi saṃśaye dharmyaśādau nirṇayasya dustyajatvāt //
children.translated_text: And there is no contradiction in a single cognition having the nature of both doubt and determination, since in every doubt whatsoever, determination regarding the <s>dharmin</s> (substratum) and so forth is impossible to abandon. //

Furthermore, this [doubt] is of many varieties based on the distinction of having two, three, four, or more alternatives; for example: 'Is this a post or a person?', 'Is the pot real, unreal, indescribable, or not indescribable?' and so forth. Likewise: 'Are these two posts or two persons?', 'Are these entities real, unreal, indescribable, or not indescribable?' and so forth. But when, regarding one of two [suspects], it is established that one is a thief, the doubt 'Is this one the thief, or is that one?' — that is a combination of two doubts of the form 'Is this one the thief or not?'

children.text:
punardvividho 'yam--- anyatarakoṭipariśeṣayogyatvatadayogyatvabhedāt /
pūrvo yathā--sthāṇvātmake vastuni sthāṇuḥ puruṣo veti /

children.translated_text: The latter, however, is illustrated by: regarding a heap of straw — 'Is it an elephant or a mountain peak?'

children.text: tatra nirūpakāṇāṃ prāyaśaḥ pūrva eva bhavati /
children.translated_text: Among these, for those who investigate, the former [type] generally occurs.
And it is through that [former type] alone that one who acts [upon it] obtains the desired object through [settling upon] one of the alternatives.

children.text: yadvā nirīhasyaiva kadācit dvitīyena saṃśayena viparyayeṇa ca pravṛttasya daivāt tadātanārthasaṃnipātenābhimatalābha iti //
children.translated_text: Or alternatively, even for one who is disinterested, sometimes through the second type of doubt or through <s>viparyaya</s> (misapprehension), acting [upon it], by the chance coincidence of the corresponding object, one may obtain the desired result. //

Furthermore, this [doubt] is of two kinds — based on the distinction between being amenable to resolution by elimination of one alternative and not being so amenable. The former is illustrated by: regarding an object that is [in fact] a post — 'Is it a post or a person?'

children.text: punarapi imau saṃśayaviparyayau sāmānyadharmiṇo viśeṣāṇāṃ cānubhūyamānatvasmaryamāṇatvādibhedāt bahuvidhāvūhanīyāviti //
children.translated_text: Furthermore, these two — <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) and <s>viparyaya</s> (error) — pertaining to the general subject and to the particulars, are of many kinds due to differences such as being directly experienced, being remembered, and so on; thus they are to be deliberated upon in manifold ways.

children.text: kiṃsajñako 'yaṃ vṛkṣa ityevamādirūpo 'nadhyavasāyo nāmānyo jñānaviśeṣa iti kecit; tadasāram, tasya saṃjñādiviśeṣasaṃdehasamanantarabhāvitadviśeṣabubhutsātmakatvāt /
children.translated_text: Some hold that there is another distinct type of cognition called <s>anadhyavasāya</s> (indetermination), of the form "By what name is this tree known?" and so on; but that is untenable, because it is of the nature of a desire to know that particular, arising immediately after the doubt regarding the particular name and so on.
Alternatively, due to the non-apprehension of the differentiating factor, it is simply <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) without a determinate alternative.

children.text: ūhastu prāyaḥ puruṣeṇānena bhavitavyamityādirūpa ekakoṭisahacaritabhūyodharmadarśanādanutkaṭānyakoṭikaḥ sa eva /
children.translated_text: <s>Ūha</s> (conjecture), on the other hand, is of the form "This is most likely a man" and so on — it is that very [doubt] in which one alternative is predominant due to the observation of a preponderance of properties associated with one alternative, while the other alternative is not prominent.

children.text: prāyaḥ puruṣeṇa bhavitavyamiti puruṣa evetyabhiprāyaścet yathocitaṃ pratyakṣānumānādiṣvanupraveśaḥ /
children.translated_text: If the meaning of "most likely a man" is understood as "it is indeed a man," then it appropriately falls within <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and other [<s>pramāṇas</s>].
We shall discuss <s>ūha</s> (conjecture) in the form of <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) under the section on <s>anumāna</s> (inference).
The <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is threefold — divided into <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony).
The blessed <s>Manu</s> also has said: "Perception, inference, and scripture of diverse traditions —
these three should be well understood by one who desires the establishment of <s>dharma</s>."
Thus.

children.text: āha ca bhagavān śaunakaḥ--- "dṛṣṭānumānāgamajaṃ dhyānasyālambanaṃ tridhā /

children.translated_text: " thus.

children.text: bhāṣyakāreṇa ca pratyakṣāditrayaṃ svaśabdenopādāya "pramāṇasaṃkhyāvivāde 'pi sarvābhyupagatapramāṇānāmayameva viṣaya iti na kenāpi pramāṇena nirviśeṣavastusiddhiḥ" ityanyeṣāmanādaraḥ kṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: And the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Rāmānuja</s>), having taken up the triad of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and so on by their own names, expressed his disregard for other [<s>pramāṇas</s>] by saying: "Even in the dispute about the number of <s>pramāṇas</s>, this alone is the domain of all universally accepted <s>pramāṇas</s> — hence no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever can establish a qualityless reality."

children.text: sarvābhyupagatapramāṇānāmiti ca parābhyupagamamātraṃ dyotayati, tatra prativādinaḥ ṣaṭpramāṇābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: And the phrase "of all universally accepted <s>pramāṇas</s>" merely indicates what is accepted by the opponents, since the opponents accept six <s>pramāṇas</s>.

children.text: pratyakṣānumānāgamānāmeva ca mitho bhedo vedārthasaṃgrahe viśadamupapāditaḥ //
children.translated_text: And the mutual distinction among <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and <s>āgama</s> (scripture) alone has been clearly established in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s>.
And the blessed <s>Śaunaka</s> has said: "The support of meditation is threefold, arising from perception, inference, and scripture —

children.text: yattu "mattaḥ smṛtijñārnamapohanaṃ ca" ityatra bhāṣyam--- "jñānamindriyaliṅgāgamayogajo vastuniścayaḥ" iti, tatrāpi yogajasya pratyakṣasya prādhānyāt pṛthagvyapadeśaḥ /

children.translated_text: And we shall discuss its subsumption [under the three <s>pramāṇas</s>].

children.text: uktaṃ ca śrīviṣṇucittaiḥ prameyasaṃgrahe--- "pramāṇasaṃkhyāvivāde 'pītyatra tripramāṇatvaṃ bhāṣyoktam" iti /
children.translated_text: And the blessed <s>Viṣṇucitta</s> has said in the <s>Prameyasaṃgraha</s>: "In the passage 'even in the dispute about the number of <s>pramāṇas</s>,' the threefold nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> is stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>."

children.text: bhāṣye ca keṣucit kośeṣu yathārthakhyātisamarthanadaśāyām--- "athavā kimanena bahunopapādanaprakāreṇa /
children.translated_text: And in certain manuscripts of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, in the context of defending <s>yathārthakhyāti</s> (the doctrine that cognition represents things as they are), [the following passage appears]: "Or what need is there of this elaborate mode of demonstration?

children.text: pratyakṣānumānāgamākhyaṃ pramāṇajātamāgamagamyaṃ ca nirastanikhiladoṣagandhamanavadhikātiśayāsaṃkhyeyakalyāṇaguṇagaṇaṃ sarvajñaṃ satyasaṃkalpaṃ paraṃ brahmābhyupagacchatāṃ kiṃ na setsyati kiṃ nopapadyate---" ityādiḥ pāṭho dṛśyate //
children.translated_text: For those who accept the supreme <s>Brahman</s> — omniscient, of infallible will, free from even the slightest trace of any defect, possessing an infinite host of immeasurable auspicious qualities — which is accessible through the group of <s>pramāṇas</s> called <s>pratyakṣa</s>, <s>anumāna</s>, and <s>āgama</s>, and which is also apprehended through scripture — what will not be accomplished, what will not be established?" — such a reading is found.

As for the <s>Bhāṣya</s> on the passage "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal" — namely, "Knowledge is the ascertainment of an object born from sense-contact, inferential mark, scripture, and <s>yoga</s>" — there too, the separate mention of <s>yoga</s>-born [knowledge] is because of the prominence of <s>yogic pratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception).

children.text:
yadyapi smṛtirapi yathārthā pramāṇamiti vakṣyate, tathāpi pratyakṣādimūlatayā tadaviśeṣāt pṛthaganuktiḥ /
uktaṃ ca tattvaratnākare --- "pratyakṣādimūlānāṃ smṛtīnāṃ svasvamūle 'ntarbhāvavivakṣayā pramāṇatritvāvirodhaḥ /

children.translated_text: And in the case of a fourfold division, a Vedic restatement has been shown" — thus.

children.text: sa cācamanuvādaḥ pūrvopāttaḥ--- "smṛtiḥ pratyakṣamaitihyamanumānaṃ catuṣṭayam" iti pratyakṣādyaviśeṣeṇa vedānuvādācca---iti /
children.translated_text: And that Vedic restatement was cited earlier: "<s>Smṛti</s>, <s>pratyakṣa</s>, <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), and <s>anumāna</s> — these four" — because it is a restatement from the <s>Veda</s> without distinction from <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the others.

children.text: prajñāparitrāṇe tu smṛtiprāmāṇyānabhyupagame 'pi jñānasya tāvat karaṇabhedāccāturvidhyamevoktam--- "tatrendriyārthasaṃbandho liṅgaśabdagrahau tathā /
children.translated_text: In the <s>Prajñāparitrāṇa</s>, however, even without accepting the validity of <s>smṛti</s> [as a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>], a fourfold classification of knowledge is stated on the basis of differences in the instrumental cause: "Among these, sense-object contact, the apprehension of an inferential mark, the apprehension of a word, and
the awakening of latent impressions — these are the generative causes of cognitions."

Although it will be stated that <s>smṛti</s> (memory), when veridical, is also a <s>pramāṇa</s>, nevertheless, since it does not differ from <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the others by virtue of being grounded in them, it is not mentioned separately.
And it has been said in the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>: "There is no contradiction with the threefold nature of <s>pramāṇa</s>, because <s>smṛtis</s> that are grounded in <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the others are subsumed under their respective sources.
Thus.
As for the passage in the same work: "Self-established [cognition], divine perception, <s>pratyakṣa</s>, <s>anumāna</s>, and <s>āgama</s> —
these five <s>pramāṇas</s> exist in the minds of <s>Jaimini</s> and <s>Vyāsa</s>."

children.text: ityādinā svayaṃsiddhidivyayoḥ pṛthaṅnirūpaṇaṃ kṛtam, tat pratyakṣāvāntaravairūpyabodhanābhiprāyam /
children.translated_text: The separate treatment of the self-established and the divine there is intended to convey the sub-varieties within <s>pratyakṣa</s>.
As the blessed <s>Viṣṇucitta</s> has said: "The divine [perception] is the <s>yogic pratyakṣa</s> obtained by the grace of the Lord."
<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, Section 12.
The Definition of <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (Perception).
In this regard, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is the valid cognition that directly apprehends [its object] (<s>sākṣātkāripramā</s>).

children.text: sākṣāttvaṃ ca jātirūpa upādhirūpo vā kaścit jñānasvabhāvaviśeṣaḥ svātmasākṣikaḥ //
children.translated_text: And <s>sākṣāttva</s> (directness) is a certain distinguishing characteristic inherent in the nature of cognition itself — whether in the form of a universal property (<s>jāti</s>) or a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) — which is self-witnessed.
A cognition that is free from being a <s>smṛti</s> (memory) born from previously known causes —
is called <s>aparokṣa</s> (non-mediate); in this definition, there is no unwanted inclusion of <s>avyāpya</s> (non-pervasive cognitions) and the like.
In the <s>Prameyasaṃgraha</s>, however, it has been stated thus: "Direct experience is <s>pratyakṣa</s>.
<s>Sākṣāttva</s> (directness) is a <s>jāti</s> (universal) —" and so on.
In the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s> too it has been stated thus: "Perception is the direct valid cognition; and the directness of a cognition is
the absence of being born from knowledge of the relation-possessor of the object that is to be dealt with."
Thus.
The dependence on an inferential mark and the like contained within that [object to be dealt with] is the <s>pārokṣya</s> (mediateness) in <s>anumāna</s> (inference) and so on."
<s>Varadaviṣṇumiśra</s>, in the <s>Mānayārthātmyanirṇaya</s>, has stated thus: "Direct valid cognition is <s>pratyakṣa</s>.
We say that the directness (<s>āparokṣya</s>) of valid cognition is the property of manifesting vividly.

children.text: kimidaṃ vaiśadyaṃ nāma ? asādhāraṇākāreṇa vastvavabhāsakatvam--" ityādi //
children.translated_text: What is this vividness? It is the capacity to reveal an object through a distinctive form that is unique to it —" and so on.
And <s>pārokṣya</s> (mediateness) has been stated thus: "<s>Pārokṣya</s> is the dependence on the cognition of an entity not contained within the object to be dealt with.

children.text:
sākṣāttvaṃ dvidhā---nityaṃ cānityaṃ car /
iśvaranityajñānādiniṣṭhaṃ nityam /
asmadādijñānaniṣṭhaṃ tvanityam /
asmadādipratyakṣaṃ dvidhā--- yogipratyakṣamayogipratyakṣaṃ ceti /
tatra yogipratyakṣaṃ prakṛṣṭādṛṣṭaviśeṣajam /
tat yuktāvasthāyāṃ manomātrajanyam /
viyuktāvasthāyāṃ tu bāhyendriyajanyamapi /
tacca bubhutsādipratiniyatamāgamaikasiddhaṃ ca /
bhāvanābalajamātraṃ jagatkartari pratyakṣaṃ pratikṣiptaṃ śāstrayonyadhikaraṇe, anyatra bhāṣyakāraireva sākṣādyogipratyakṣasya kaṇṭhokteḥ, tasya saṃbhavato 'pyāgamikeśvarajñānamūlasyāgamānuvādatvāpādanāśaktyā tatraudāsīnyāt, dharmādayaḥ kasyacidindriyagrāhyāḥ, prameyatvāt, ghaṭavat, mīmāṃsakānāmapratyakṣatvādvā, asmatsukhādivadityādyanumānānāṃ vipakṣe bādhakavirahādibhirābhāsatvāt, āgamabādhaprasaṅgasyaiva puraskāre tvāgamenaiva caritārthatvāt; anyathā dharmādayaḥ kasyaciccakṣurgrāhyā iti vadato bauddhasya kiṃ prativakṣyasi /
yaścānuvyavasāye saviṣayavyavasāyapratyakṣatāmicchati, tasyāsmadādiṣvapi dharmādivyavasāyānuvyavasāye dharmādipratyakṣatvasiddhau kathaṃ tadatiriktayogipratyakṣānumāsiddhiḥ /
tadvyavacchedena prayoge /
api saugatoktacākṣuṣatvādisādhanaprasaṅga syāditi /

children.translated_text: And that special <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) arises from the practice of <s>yoga</s>, austerity, and other [spiritual disciplines].

Therefore, even what is accepted by the seers (<s>ārṣa</s>) is subsumed under that [yogic perception] alone, since there is no difference in its being born from a special kind of extraordinary <s>adṛṣṭa</s>.
As it has been said in the <s>Prajñāparitrāṇa</s>: "Here, the knowledge that illuminates objects without depending on the sense organs —
the knowers of <s>pramāṇa</s> call that divine <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).

<s>Sākṣāttva</s> (directness) is of two kinds — eternal and non-eternal.
That which pertains to the eternal cognition of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) and so on is eternal.
That which pertains to the cognitions of ourselves and others is non-eternal.
The <s>pratyakṣa</s> of ourselves and others is of two kinds — <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception) and <s>ayogipratyakṣa</s> (non-yogic perception).
Among these, <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> arises from a special kind of extraordinary <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit).
In the state of <s>yoga</s> (meditative union), it is produced by the mind alone.
In the state of separation [from <s>yoga</s>], it may also be produced by the external sense organs.
And it is regulated by the particular desire to know, and is established solely through <s>āgama</s> (scripture).
Mere <s>pratyakṣa</s> of the world-creator arising from the force of meditation alone was rejected in the <s>Śāstrayoni</s> ("Scripture is the source") <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, because the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Rāmānuja</s>) himself has explicitly affirmed <s>yogic pratyakṣa</s> elsewhere; and because, even though such [yogic perception] is possible, since it is rooted in scriptural knowledge of <s>Īśvara</s>, one cannot reduce it to a mere restatement of <s>āgama</s>, hence there is indifference [to it] there; <s>dharma</s> and other [supersensible entities] are perceptible to some, because they are objects of valid knowledge, like a pot — and the argument that [<s>dharma</s> is] non-perceptible for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, or like our own pleasure and so on — such inferences are fallacious due to the absence of a defeater in the counter-example and other [defects]; and if the threat of scriptural contradiction is given priority, then scripture itself suffices [to establish the point].
Otherwise, what will you say in response to the Buddhist who claims that <s>dharma</s> and other [supersensible entities] are visually perceptible to some?
And for one who holds that in the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> (reflective cognition), the perceptual nature of the object-directed <s>vyavasāya</s> (determinate cognition) [is established] — for such a person, even in our own case, through the reflective cognition of the determinate cognition of <s>dharma</s> and the like, the perceptibility of <s>dharma</s> would be established; so how can the inference for a <s>yogic pratyakṣa</s> beyond that be established?
In formulating the argument to exclude that,
the same fallacy of proving what the Buddhist claims — namely visual perceptibility and so on — would arise.
The cognition of the supreme Lord, and likewise the cognitions of the liberated souls,
and also the seer-cognitions of <s>Saṃjaya</s>, <s>Arjuna</s>, <s>Vālmīki</s>, and others — those too [are divine <s>pramāṇa</s>]."
Thus.

children.text:
indriyānapekṣamiti---adivyenrdiyānapekṣamityarthaḥ /
ata eva hi gīyate--- "divyaṃ dadāmi te cakṣuḥ---" ityādi /
yadvāparameśvarādivijñānasahapāṭhādibhistathaiva mantavyam /

children.translated_text: And immediately after, it has been stated thus: "Of the natural knowledge that of itself illuminates all things,
the obstruction is due to <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and the impediment [to its manifestation] is from contact with the sense organs.
For the liberated souls, through the removal of <s>avidyā</s>, their cognitions
illuminate all objects in their natural form.

"Without depending on the sense organs" means without depending on non-divine sense organs.
For precisely this reason it is proclaimed: "I give you the divine eye —" and so on.
Alternatively, from the co-enumeration with the cognition of the supreme Lord and so on, it should be understood in that very way.
The cognition of the <s>ṛṣis</s> (seers), which is favored
by the Supreme [Lord] who serves as the counteragent to the state of obstruction, illuminates all things."
Thus.

children.text: mānasapratyakṣamapyasmadādīnāṃ nāstyeveti vṛddhasaṃpradāyaḥ, ātmasvarūpasya taddharmabhūtajñānasya ca svayaṃprakāśatvāt, sukhaduḥkhecchādveṣaprayatnānāṃ tattaddhetutayābhimatajñānaviśeṣānatirekasya vedārthasaṃgrahe samarthitatvāt, nityatvādiviśiṣṭāsmadādyanubhavasya śāstrādiprasiddhatvāt, pūrvānubhavādijñānasya smṛtirūpatvāt, "ātmasukhādivyatiriktabahirviṣayeṣu tasya bāhyendriyānapekṣapravṛttyanupapatteḥ" iti śāstrayonyadhikaraṇabhāṣyasyānvāroheṇāpyupapatteriti //
children.translated_text: The tradition of the elders holds that <s>mānasa pratyakṣa</s> (mental perception) does not exist at all for us ordinary beings — because the self in its essential nature and its attributive consciousness (<s>dharmabhūtajñāna</s>) are self-luminous; because the non-difference of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort from the particular cognitions considered to be their respective causes has been demonstrated in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s>; because our experience of [the self] as qualified by eternality and other attributes is well-known from scripture and other sources; because cognition of prior experience and the like is of the nature of <s>smṛti</s> (memory); and because this is also consistent with the <s>Bhāṣya</s> on the <s>Śāstrayoni adhikaraṇa</s>, which states: "Because there is no possibility of its functioning independently of the external sense organs with regard to external objects other than the self, pleasure, and the like."
Therefore, knowledge produced by non-divine external sense organs is <s>ayogipratyakṣa</s> (non-yogic perception).

That is produced by sense organs assisted by general <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit), light, and other auxiliary factors, and has a determinate range of objects due to the specific configuration of the operative conditions.
It is fivefold, due to the differences in the distinctive causal factors unique to the ear and other sense organs.

children.text: viṣayendriyasaṃbandhaśca---dravyeṣu saṃyogaḥ, dravyāśriteṣu rūpādiṣu tu saṃyuktāśrayaṇam /
children.translated_text: And the relation between the object and the sense organ is: in the case of substances, conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>); in the case of qualities such as color and the like, which inhere in substances, it is the relation of having a conjoined substrate (<s>saṃyuktāśrayaṇa</s>).

children.text: yathoktaṃ tattvaratnākare--- "atra vṛddhā vidāmāsuḥ saṃyogaḥ saṃnikarṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: As it has been said in the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>: "Here the elders have declared: conjunction is the sense-contact;
and the relation of having a conjoined substrate — let these be understood as applicable in their respective cases."
Thus.
Furthermore, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is of two kinds — <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate) and <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate).
<s>Savikalpaka</s> (determinate perception) is perception accompanied by <s>pratyavamarśa</s> (reflective judgment).
<s>Nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate perception) is perception devoid of that [reflective judgment].
<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, Section 13.
Refutation of the <s>Naiyāyika</s> (logician's) conception of <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate perception).

children.text: bālamūkatiryagādivijñānamapi hi saṃjñāvikalparahitamapi viśiṣṭavastuviṣayameva, anyathā teṣāṃ heyopādeyavibhāgapūrvakapravṛttiśeṣānupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: For even the cognitions of infants, mute persons, and animals, though devoid of name-based conceptualization, have only qualified objects; otherwise their purposeful activity presupposing the discrimination of what is to be avoided and what is to be pursued would be inexplicable.

children.text: vipratipannaṃ viśiṣṭajñānaṃ viśeṣaṇajñānapūrvakam, viśiṣṭajñānatvāt, surabhi candanamityādiviśiṣṭajñānavaditi cenna, ekasāmagrīvedyaviśeṣaṇeṣu tannirapekṣatvāt, svarūpasaṃbandhapakṣe svarūpagraheṇaiva saṃbandhasyāpi grahaṇāt, tāvataiva viśiṣṭagrahaṇasiddheḥ, samavāyavāde 'pi tasyaiva gṛhyamāṇasya viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvarūpatvāt, samavāyaviśiṣṭapratyaye tathaivābhyupagamāt, tadvaiśiṣṭyagrahe ca guṇavaiśiṣṭyagrahasyāvarjanīyatvāt /
children.translated_text: If it be argued that qualified cognition (<s>viśiṣṭajñāna</s>) requires prior cognition of the qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>), because it is a qualified cognition, just like the qualified cognition "fragrant sandalwood" and so on — that is not so, because in the case of qualifiers cognizable through a single operative complex, there is no such dependence; in the <s>svarūpasaṃbandha</s> (intrinsic-relation) view, the relation is grasped by the very grasping of the essential nature, and that alone suffices for the grasping of the qualified entity; even in the <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) view, that very [inherence] which is being grasped is itself of the nature of the qualifier-qualified relation; and since in the cognition qualified by <s>samavāya</s>, it is accepted in precisely that way, the grasping of that qualification inevitably entails the grasping of the qualification by the quality.

children.text: na ca samavāyasya savikalpakaikaviṣayateti vācyam, nirvikalpake dharmavaddharmivacca tatsaṃbandhasyāpyaindriyikatvāviśeṣeṇa grahaṇasaṃbhavāt, yogyasya saṃnikṛṣṭagṛhyamāṇasaṃbandhinaḥ saṃbandhasyāgrahaṇānupapatteḥ, anyathā nityaṃ tadagrahāpātāt /
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that <s>samavāya</s> is an object only of <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate perception), because in <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate perception) there is the possibility of grasping [<s>samavāya</s>] too — just as with the property and the property-bearer — since it is equally sensory in nature; because it is untenable that a relation of what is fit [to be cognized] and is in contact [with the sense organ] should not be grasped; otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence of its never being grasped.

children.text: prathamākṣasaṃnipātajā buddhirviśiṣṭaviṣayā, buddhitvāt, saṃpratipannavat, ityādyapi cintyam //
children.translated_text: The argument that "the cognition born from the first contact of the sense organ has a qualified object, because it is a cognition, like an accepted instance" — this too is to be critically examined.
Both types [of perception] have only qualified objects (<s>viśiṣṭaviṣaya</s>), because a cognition that grasps an unqualified object is neither observed nor logically tenable.
<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, Section 14.
An Exposition of <s>Savikalpaka</s> (Determinate Perception).

children.text: na ca savikalpakaṃ na pratyakṣamiti vācyam, sākṣātkārābādhādyaviśeṣāt //
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate perception) is not <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), because there is no difference in [possessing] directness (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>), non-sublation, and other [characteristics of perception].
Due to a difference in auxiliary causes, there arises no difference in kind;
but within the same kind, some difference may indeed occur.
Where a difference in kind is seen, it may be accepted in that case;
but on that basis alone, such an attribution should not be made everywhere.
And no cognition whatsoever is accepted as produced by a sense organ alone;
for cognitions are differentiated per sense organ by their specific auxiliary causes.
Therefore, even when there is a contribution of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), by virtue of possessing directness (<s>aparokṣatva</s>),
the perceptual nature of <s>vikalpa</s> (determinate cognition) is never negated in any case.

children.text: "nirvikalpakamekajātīyeṣu dravyeṣu prathamapiṇḍagrahaṇam" ityādibhāṣyaṃ tu udāharaṇaparaṃ yojyam /
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṣya</s> statement that "<s>nirvikalpaka</s> is the first apprehension of an individual among objects of the same class" and so on should be construed as illustrative.

children.text: ata eva hi śrīviṣṇucittairuktam--- "saṃskārodbodhasahakṛtendriyajanyaṃ jñānaṃ savikalpakam, ekajātīyeṣu prathamapiṇḍagrahaṇam dvitīyādipiṇḍagrahaṇeṣu prathamākṣasaṃnipātajaṃ ca jñānaṃ nirvikalpakam" iti /
children.translated_text: For precisely this reason the blessed <s>Viṣṇucitta</s> has said: "Cognition produced by a sense organ assisted by the awakening of latent impressions is <s>savikalpaka</s>; the first apprehension of an individual among objects of the same class, and the cognition born of the first contact of the sense organ in the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals, is <s>nirvikalpaka</s>."
And elsewhere it has been said: "That which is produced by the sense organ of sight and the like alone is <s>nirvikalpaka</s>" and so on.
As for what has been said in the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>: "In <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate perception), there is the exclusion of qualifiers from their own inherence alone;
in <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate perception), there is the exclusion from association with other [objects], and it is also characterized by naming."
In that passage too, the intent should be taken as merely illustrating the absence and presence of dependence on latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>).

children.text: pratyakṣasya caivaṃ vibhāgo 'bhihitaḥ--- "dvividhaṃ caitat pratyakṣam--- arvācīnamanarvācīnaṃ ca /
children.translated_text: And the division of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) has been stated thus: "And this <s>pratyakṣa</s> is of two kinds — limited (<s>arvācīna</s>) and unlimited (<s>anarvācīna</s>).
That which is capable of simultaneously directly apprehending all objects without exception is <s>anarvācīna</s> (unlimited).
It shall be demonstrated that this belongs to <s>yogins</s>, liberated souls, and the Lord, and depends on their special power" — and so on.

children.text:
ata eva kudṛṣṭīnāṃ sanmātragrāhi pratyakṣamityavilakṣajalpitaṃ nirastam /
kramayaugapadyādidūṣaṇaṃ tu bhrāntivikalpe 'pi samānam /
bhrāntirūpo 'pi hi vikalpaḥ kṣaṇikatvānna viramya vyāpartumalam /
na ca pūrvajñānavārtāṃ jānāti /
na ca svayaṃ dharmipratiyogigrahaṇābhāve bhedagrahaṇaṃ manyase /
tathāpi yadi kalpanā bhedaviśiṣṭaṃ yugapadgṛhṇāti, kā pratyakṣe sarpamṛtiḥ ? ato dharmivadyogyatvājjātyādirūpabhedo 'pi yugapadgrāhyeḥ /
abheda iva bhedo 'pi svarūpataḥ pratītau na pratiyogisākāṅkṣaḥ; bhedavyavahārastvabhedavyavahāravat tatsākāṅkṣa /
ataḥ prathamameva bhedadhīryuktā /
ata eva dharmadharmiṇordharmipratiyoginoranyeṣāṃ ca pratītāvanyonyāśrayo nirastaḥ /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, the charge of mutual dependence (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>) in the cognition of property and property-bearer (<s>dharma</s> and <s>dharmin</s>), of the property-bearer and its counter-correlate, and of other such pairs, is refuted.
And consequently, even in the verbal usage arising from linguistic convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>), the same objection does not arise.

children.text: bhedaśabdena vyavahārasya tu pratisaṃbandhinirūpitākāre vyutpannatvāt tadapekṣā /
children.translated_text: However, for the verbal usage employing the word 'difference' (<s>bheda</s>), since one's linguistic competence is established with respect to the form determined by each relatum (<s>pratisaṃbandhin</s>), there is dependence on that.

children.text: bhedatvaṃ hi bhedānāṃ pratiyoginā nirūpyam na tu jātyādilakṣaṇaṃ svarūpam; yadgraho yatra yadāropavirodhī, sa hi tasya tasmādbhedaḥ; gotvādi ca gṛhyamāṇaṃ svasmin svāśraye cāśvatvādyāropaṃ nirūṇaddhīti svasya svāśrayasya ca svayameva tasmādbhedaḥ //
children.translated_text: For the nature of being a difference (<s>bhedatva</s>) among differences is to be determined by the counter-correlate, but not the intrinsic nature characterized by universal (<s>jāti</s>) and the like. That apprehension which, in a given locus, is opposed to the superimposition of something else — that indeed is the difference of that thing from that other. And universals such as <s>gotva</s> (cow-ness) and the like, when apprehended, themselves negate the superimposition of horse-ness (<s>aśvatva</s>) etc. upon themselves and upon their substrata — thus they themselves are the difference of themselves and their substrata from that other.

Therefore, the incoherent babbling of the heterodox (<s>kudṛṣṭi</s>) that perception grasps mere being (<s>sanmātra</s>) is refuted. The objection based on sequence and simultaneity (<s>krama</s> and <s>yaugapadya</s>) applies equally even to erroneous <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition). For even a <s>vikalpa</s> that is of the nature of error, being momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), cannot cease and then operate again; nor does it know the content of the prior cognition. And you do not hold that there can be apprehension of difference (<s>bheda</s>) without apprehension of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) and counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogin</s>). Even so, if conceptualization (<s>kalpanā</s>) grasps what is qualified by difference all at once, what obstacle is there for perception? Therefore, just as the property-bearer is capable of being grasped, so too difference in the form of universal (<s>jāti</s>) and the like is to be grasped simultaneously. Just as non-difference (<s>abheda</s>), so too difference (<s>bheda</s>) in its own nature does not require a counter-correlate for being cognized; but the verbal usage of difference, like that of non-difference, does require it. Therefore, the cognition of difference is justified from the very outset.

children.text: api ca pratiyogisāpekṣatvanirapekṣatvalakṣaṇaviruddhadharmādhyāsena bhedāt svarūpabhedagrahaṇaikyāṃ na saṃbhavatīti vadan bhedaduṣaṇārthameva bhedaṃ sādhayatīti svavacanavirodha iti //
children.translated_text: Moreover, one who says that the apprehension of intrinsic difference and of difference [as requiring a counter-correlate] cannot be identical, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties — namely, dependence on a counter-correlate and independence thereof — actually establishes difference for the very purpose of refuting difference, and thus contradicts his own statement.
<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Pratyakṣādhyāya</s>, section 15.
Refutation of verbal non-mediate cognition (<s>śābdāparokṣa</s>).

children.text:
śabdajanyamapi pratyakṣamastīti ta eva varṇayanti; tadapyayuktam, vyāghātāt /
na hi parokṣajananasvabhāvatayā siddhā sāmagrī viśeṣābhāve kvacit svabhāvamatipatet /
na caikajātīyasāmagrītaḥ prasūtaṃ kāryaṃ vicitraṃ syāt, ekayaivava sāmagryā sarvajātīyotpattiprasaṅgāt ekasya kāryasya viruddhajātiyogaprasaṅgācca /
"daśamastvamasi" ityādidṛṣṭānte 'pi tvamarthamātraṃ pratyakṣam /
'daśamo 'ham' iti pratyayo hi nendriyasvātantryeṇodeti, kintu puruṣavacanānurodhena /
tanmūle 'pi cet pratyakṣatā, evam 'dharmavāṃstvamasi' iti kārtāntikopadeśādau 'tādṛśo 'hamasmi' iti bodhe dharmāderapi pratyakṣatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
tataścāpratyakṣamiti jagati kiñcinna syāt, pratyakṣabhūtaṃ yatkiñciduddiśya viśeṣaṇatayaiva sarvasya pratyakṣatvopapatteḥ /
