pūrvāvagatadaśamabhāvaṃ tu puruṣaṃ pratyupadeśe bhāṣarāśipraviṣṭamaṣīnyāyena pūrvāparāparokṣaṇīnairantaryeṇa madhyavartiśabdajanyadhiyo 'parokṣatvavyavahāraḥ kasyacit syādvā na vā /

ata eva tattvamasyādiśabdaḥ svaviṣayagocarapratyakṣajñānajanakaḥ, svato 'parokṣārthagocaratvāt "daśamastvamasi" "saṃvit svaprakāśā" ityādivākyavat ityādyanumānāni nirastāni, daśamatvasvaprakāśatvādiviśiṣṭākāreṇa dṛṣṭānteṣvaparokṣajñānajananāsiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, arguments such as 'The statement <s>tattvamasi</s> ("That thou art") and the like generates perceptual knowledge regarding its own domain of reference, because it has as its object what is intrinsically non-mediate — just like the statements "You are the tenth" and "Consciousness is self-luminous"' are refuted, because it is not established that in the illustrative examples, non-mediate knowledge is generated with the specific qualified form of being-the-tenth, self-luminosity, and so on.

children.text: tathā vigītaḥ śabdo na svavācyagocarapratyakṣadhījanakaḥ, śabdatvāt, saṃpratipannavat, ityādyapipratiprayoktavyam /
children.translated_text: Likewise, the counter-argument should be advanced: 'A word whose [capacity] is disputed is not a generator of perceptual cognition regarding its own referent, because it is a word — like a word whose [capacity] is accepted [by both parties].'

In this regard, the absurd consequences of contradiction with apprehension, confusion of the definitions of verbal testimony and perception, and so forth serve as invalidators (<s>bādhaka</s>) against the opponent's position.

This does not [apply] to the former [i.e., our position], because even without perception generated by verbal testimony, the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) is attained through direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) produced by yogic or unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), or else through the will (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) of the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>) propitiated by a special act of meditation (<s>praṇidhāna</s>).

Those same [opponents] maintain that there exists a perception generated by verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>). That too is unjustified, because of contradiction. For a causal complex established as having the nature of generating mediate cognition (<s>parokṣa</s>) cannot, in the absence of any distinguishing factor, abandon its nature in some cases. Nor can an effect produced from a causal complex of a single kind be of varied types, since from one and the same complex there would be the absurd consequence of producing effects of every kind, and of a single effect being connected with contradictory kinds. Even in the illustrative example 'You are the tenth' (<s>daśamastvamasi</s>), only the meaning of 'you' is perceptual. For the cognition 'I am the tenth' does not arise through the independence of the senses, but rather in accordance with the statement of a person. And if even what is rooted in that [verbal statement] has the status of perception, then by the same reasoning, from the instruction of an astrologer saying 'You are virtuous,' in the cognition 'I am of such a nature,' even <s>dharma</s> and the like would absurdly become perceptual. Then nothing in the world would be non-perceptual, since everything could be justified as perceptual merely by being a qualifier of something that is itself perceptually given. As for the person who, prior to the instruction, was unaware of being the tenth — when he enters the range of discourse, by the principle of ink-drops (<s>maṣīnyāya</s>), through the continuity of what is immediately cognized before and after, the usage of 'non-mediate' (<s>aparokṣa</s>) for the cognition born of the intervening word may or may not obtain for someone.

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ cidacinmayaṃ jagadidaṃ yasyetyanuśrūyate yaścānanyadhiyāmanantavibhavaḥ pratyakṣatāmaśnute /
children.translated_text: He of whom it is heard in scripture that this world, consisting of sentient (<s>cit</s>) and non-sentient (<s>acit</s>) beings, is His perception, and He who, being of infinite glory, attains the status of being directly perceived through the cognition of non-difference,

children.text: yaścaiko yugapatsadā svata idaṃ viśvaṃ darīdṛśyate prājñaṃ taṃ pratipannamokṣaṇavidhādakṣaṃ didṛkṣemahi //
children.translated_text: And He who alone, always, by His own nature, simultaneously perceives this entire universe — may we desire to behold that omniscient One, through the method of attaining liberation that has been established! [Verse]

children.text: iti śrīkavitārkikasiṃhasya sarvatantrasvatantrasya śrīmadveṅkaṭanāthasya vedāntācāryasya kṛtiṣu nyāyapariśuddhau pratyakṣādhyāye dvitīyamāhnikam //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second session (<s>āhnika</s>) of the <s>Pratyakṣādhyāya</s> (Chapter on Perception) in the <s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, among the works of the venerable <s>Veṅkaṭanātha</s>, the <s>Vedāntācārya</s>, the lion among poets and logicians (<s>kavitārkikasiṃha</s>), independent master of all systems (<s>sarvatantrasvatantra</s>).
And the <s>Pratyakṣādhyāya</s> (Chapter on Perception) is concluded.
Salutation to the glorious <s>Nigamāntamahādeśika</s> (the great teacher of the end of the <s>Vedas</s>)!
Now begins the <s>Śabdādhyāya</s> (Chapter on Verbal Testimony).

children.text: nyā. pa. śa. 1 athānumodayaṃ smṛtyā hetutvenāpi saṃsthitm /
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Śabdādhyāya</s>, section 1. Now, [the means of valid knowledge] which is established as a cause alongside memory (<s>smṛti</s>), which follows upon [perception and inference],
That <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) as a means of valid knowledge (<s>māna</s>), situated between those two [i.e., perception and inference], we shall now expound.

children.text:
anāptānuktavākyajanitaṃ tadarthavijñānaṃ tat pramāṇam; kāraṇadoṣabādhakādarśanāt /
nacānāptoktavākyaṃ pramāṇaṃ, kāraṇadoṣabādhakadarśanāt, na ca vākyatvādibhirbādhaḥ; svavacanavirodhāt /
yadi bādhakopanyāsavākyamayathārthaṃ, tadā kathaṃ bādhaḥ /
atha yathārtham, tasyāpi pakṣīkāre tadbādhaḥ /
bahiṣkāre tenaivānaikāntyam /
na cātiprasaṅgaḥ; bhrāntādivākyānāṃ doṣamūlatvasya durapahnavatvāt /

children.translated_text: But here [in the case of trustworthy testimony] such [defect] is absent.

As for [apparent instances such as] letters formed by termites in a dream and the like — since they are unreliable due to the absence of a specific intended purport (<s>tātparya</s>), even though they may convey meaning, and since deviation is observed [in such cases].
Even in the case of the eternal <s>Veda</s>, which has the nature of the eternal command of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), the intended purport with respect to the various meanings does not lapse.

children.text: tasya cātrābhāvāt, kvācitkadoṣadarśanasya ca pratyakṣādāvapi asamatvāt, svataḥ parato vā prāmāṇye ca tato viśeṣābhāvāt //
children.translated_text: And since such [defect] is absent here, and since the observation of occasional defects does not equally apply to perception and the like, and since there is no distinction between the two [positions] whether validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is intrinsic (<s>svataḥ</s>) or extrinsic (<s>parataḥ</s>).

The cognition of the meaning of a sentence uttered by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is that <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge); because no defect in the cause or invalidator (<s>bādhaka</s>) is observed. A sentence uttered by an untrustworthy person is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because a defect in the cause or an invalidator is observed. Nor is there invalidation merely by virtue of being a sentence and so on, for that would contradict one's own statement. If the sentence adducing the invalidator is itself not veridical, then how can there be invalidation? If, on the other hand, it is veridical, then if it too is included in the thesis, it is invalidated by that. If it is excluded, then by that very fact there is inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntya</s>). Nor is there over-extension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>), because it is undeniable that sentences of the deluded and the like have their root in defects.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 2 tacca vedyāṃśe pratyakṣātiriktam, asākṣātkāritvāt, anumānavat /
anumānātiriktaṃ, pakṣaliṅgaparāmarśādyadṛṣṭeḥ, padavākyatatsaṃbandhādīnāṃ ca viśiṣṭavākyārthaṃ pratyasiddhavyāptikatvenāliṅgatvāt, dṛṣṭāntābhyupagame sarvatrāviśeṣāt, vyutpattau ca svatantratayaiva bodhakatvasiddheḥ /
ata eva vaktṛjñānānumānābhyupagamepi śabdaprāmāṇyaṃ siddham /
āgamikabuddhiranumā, pratyakṣetarapramititvāt, saṃpratipannavaditi cenna, uktottaratvāt /
anyathā śabdarasagandhādi buddhiranumā, acākṣuṣapramititvāt, saṃpratipannavat, ityapi prasaṅgāt /
"pratyakṣamanumānaṃ ca śāstraṃ ca vividhāgamam /
dṛṣṭānumānāgamajam" iti manvādimaharṣisaṃmateśca śabdānumānayorbhedodṛśyate /

children.translated_text: Nor is the principle of inclusion of the ox under the bull (<s>gobalīvardanyāya</s>) applicable here, since inclusion is not observed.

children.text: āgāmonumānaṃ, saṃbandhagrahaṇe satyeva bodhakatvāditi cenna; bodhya bodhakabhāvātiriktasaṃbandhagrahaṇāpekṣiṇyanumānatvaniyamāt /
children.translated_text: If it is said that scripture is inference because it conveys meaning only when the relation [between word and meaning] has been grasped — this is not so, because there is a restriction that inference requires the grasping of a relation over and above the relation of object-to-be-known and means-of-knowing.

children.text: na cātra tadatiriktaḥ saṃbandhaḥ, yadgrahaṇaṃ niyamenāpekṣyeta /
children.translated_text: And here there is no relation beyond [that of word and meaning] the grasping of which would be necessarily required.
Otherwise, since by virtue of requiring a relation, even the perceptual status of those two [i.e., word and meaning] could easily be established [as inference, which is absurd].

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Śabdādhyāya</s>, section 2. And that [verbal testimony], with respect to the object to be known, is distinct from perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), because it is non-immediate (<s>asākṣātkārin</s>), like inference (<s>anumāna</s>). It is distinct from inference, because the inferential process involving thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), mark (<s>liṅga</s>), and subsumptive reflection (<s>parāmarśa</s>) is not observed [in the case of verbal testimony]; and because words (<s>pada</s>), sentences (<s>vākya</s>), their relations, and the like, not having established pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) with respect to the qualified sentence-meaning, are not inferential marks (<s>liṅga</s>); and because if illustrative examples were conceded [for such an inference], there would be no distinction anywhere; and because in linguistic convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>), the capacity to convey meaning is established independently. For this very reason, even if the inference of the speaker's knowledge is conceded, the validity of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is established. And if it is objected that cognition from scripture (<s>āgamika</s>) is inference because it is a valid cognition other than perception — like the accepted [case of inference] — this is not so, because this has already been answered. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that cognition of sound, taste, smell, and so on is inference, because it is a valid cognition that is non-visual — like the accepted [case]. Moreover, in the statements of great sages like <s>Manu</s> and others — 'Perception, inference, and scripture, and the manifold tradition; born of direct experience, inference, and tradition' — the distinction between verbal testimony and inference is clearly seen.

children.text:
na ca smṛtiḥ; apūrvaviṣayatvāt /
padasaṃdohaviśeṣo vākyam /
prāmāṇikapadavyavahāraviṣayaḥ padam /
tasya suptiṅantatvādikalpanayāpi vyaktiḥ kriyate /
ata eva hyanyathānyathā prakṛtipratyayādikaṃ vyākaraṇāntareṣu kalpyate /
tacca na sāṃketikam; saṃketayitṛpuruṣāsaṃbhavāt /
ata eva na bhāṣāntaravat tatklaptiḥ, nityavedagatatvācca /
yāni vaidikāni padāni tānyeva laukikanīti "vedaśabdebhya evādau" ityādivacanādapi siddham /
children.translated_text: That the very words found in the <s>Veda</s> are the same as those in common usage is established also from the statement 'From the words of the <s>Veda</s> itself in the beginning' and the like.

The difference in grammatical rules between the spoken language (<s>bhāṣā</s>) and the Vedic language (<s>chandas</s>) pertains to the restriction of particular word-sequences (<s>ānupūrvī</s>) for certain words only.
Every word used in the spoken language has its usage somewhere in the <s>Veda</s>.
The settled position is that no word is restricted exclusively to the <s>Veda</s> and found nowhere else.

Nor is it memory (<s>smṛti</s>), because it has a novel object. A sentence (<s>vākya</s>) is a particular collection of words (<s>pada</s>). A word (<s>pada</s>) is the object of valid linguistic usage. Its manifestation is achieved even through the postulation of ending in nominal (<s>sup</s>) or verbal (<s>tiṅ</s>) suffixes. For this very reason, the analysis of roots (<s>prakṛti</s>), suffixes (<s>pratyaya</s>), and so on is variously formulated in different grammars. And this [word-meaning relation] is not conventional (<s>sāṃketika</s>), because of the impossibility of a person who could have established the convention. For this very reason, its formulation is not like that of other languages, and because it is found in the eternal <s>Veda</s>.

children.text: uktaṃ caitadvedārthasaṃgrahepi--- "vaidikā eva sarve vācakāḥ śabdāśca---" ityādinā //
children.translated_text: And this has been stated also in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s> — 'All significatory words are indeed Vedic —' and so on.

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Śabdādhyāya</s>, section 3. Sentences (<s>vākya</s>) are of two kinds — due to the distinction between those authored by a person (<s>pauruṣeya</s>) and those not authored by a person (<s>apauruṣeya</s>).
That which is characterized by a particular composition dependent on the free will of a person is <s>pauruṣeya</s> (person-authored).

children.text: taddvidhā, anvitārthamananvitārthaṃ ca, ādyaṃ yathā---agniruṣṇaḥ, āpo dravāḥ, iti /
children.translated_text: That is of two kinds: having a coherent meaning (<s>anvitārtha</s>) and having an incoherent meaning (<s>ananvitārtha</s>). The first is illustrated by: 'Fire is hot,' 'Waters are fluid.'
The second is illustrated by: 'Fire is not hot,' 'Waters are hard.'

children.translated_text: 'Or alternatively, let it be merely reiterative.',
'For verbal testimony is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding an object already cognized by another means of knowledge.',

children.text: tathaiva hi tasya vyutpattiḥ" ityuktvā "nanvanuvādakatayaiva vyutpattiḥ puṃvākyeṣu" ityādinā vaktṛjñānānumānamupapādya "satyam, daivāt tadanuvādakatvamiti nābuddhabodhanasvārasyabhaṅgaprasaṅgaḥ, yathā smṛtyanumitavedasyānuvādakatvepyarthāditi na mānatābhaṅgaḥ" ityādi uktaṃ ca prajñāparitrāṇe --- "pauruṣeyagiraḥ śaṅkāgrastā na sahasā mitim /
children.translated_text: 'For its linguistic convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>) is indeed like that' — having said this, and having then established the inference of the speaker's knowledge through [the passage beginning with] 'But the linguistic convention in the case of human sentences is indeed as merely reiterative,' [the <s>Vivaraṇa</s> author continues:] 'True, but its being reiterative is incidental (<s>daivāt</s>), so there is no danger of breaking the natural capacity of revealing what is not known; just as even when the <s>Veda</s> inferred from <s>smṛti</s> is reiterative, there is no loss of its validity.' And it has been stated in the <s>Prajñāparitrāṇa</s>: 'Sentences of human origin, being subject to doubt, do not immediately produce valid cognition,
So long as there is no apprehension of another [valid] means of knowledge underlying them.

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Śabdādhyāya</s>, section 4. Here, some partial adherents (<s>ekadeśin</s>) say: Since there is non-apprehension of coherence (<s>anvaya</s>), the usage of coherence arises only sometimes. For this very reason, from a worldly sentence in which deviation has been observed, there is no immediate ascertainment of the sentence-meaning from the sentence, because it requires deliberation on compatibility (<s>yogyatā</s>). Even when general compatibility is apprehended, since the compatibility with respect to the particular instance cannot be established without inference of the speaker's knowledge — this has been demonstrated in the <s>Prameyasaṃgraha</s> and other works. Similarly, in order to refute [the view that] perception grasps mere being (<s>sanmātra</s>), when the absurd consequence arises that scripture would be merely reiterative (<s>anuvādaka</s>), the author of the <s>Vivaraṇa</s> has stated: 'The purport is that it would be a defect if verbal testimony, whose natural function is to reveal what is not [otherwise] known (<s>abuddhabodhana</s>), were to be otherwise.'
And having inferred another valid means of knowledge capable of grounding the speaker's [assertion],
One ascertains the sentence-meaning through the inferential mark of the statement made by that [speaker].
This sentence is always fit for expressing a coherent meaning,

children.text: asau ca nānṛtaṃ vakti saṃjñātvārthaṃ tadabravīt //
children.translated_text: And that [speaker] does not speak falsely — having known the meaning, he stated it.
Through the inference of the speaker's knowledge, from one's own sentence whose [content] is known or unknown,
The cognition of the mere fitness of sentences to express a coherent meaning —
This inferential process (<s>parāmarśa</s>) that arises does not have the connection of meanings as its object.
Non-contradiction with other means of knowledge is what is called compatibility (<s>yogyatā</s>).

children.text: nanvevaṃ laukikaṃ vākyaṃ liṅgaṃ celliṅgavat tataḥ /
children.translated_text: But if so, then a worldly sentence would be an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>), and like an inferential mark, accordingly,
Since a word [conveys meaning] from its grasped relation, it too would have the status of an inferential mark.',
'At the time of learning the linguistic convention, for the one learning, there is certainly no inferential cognition.',
'If it be said that words, [even] without [prior] linguistic convention, are capable of conveying meaning — then from this,
Meaning-cognition would arise intrinsically, and thus it would not at all have the status of an inferential mark.'

children.translated_text: In the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s> as well, this has been elaborated in detail, preceded by the section on the validity of scripture (<s>āgamaprāmāṇya</s>).

children.text: apauruṣeyaṃ tu sarvamanvitārthamevākintu ādityo yūpaḥ-- ityādiṣūpacārato nirvāhaḥ /
children.translated_text: As for the <s>apauruṣeya</s> (unauthored, i.e., the <s>Veda</s>), all of it has a coherent meaning (<s>anvitārtha</s>) only. However, in cases such as '<s>Āditya</s> is the sacrificial post (<s>yūpa</s>),' the resolution is through figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>).

children.text: ākāṅkṣāsattivogyatāvanti hi padānyanvitamabhidadhati, anvaye vā viśrāmyanti /
children.translated_text: For words that possess expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), contiguity (<s>satti</s>), and compatibility (<s>yogyatā</s>) express a connected meaning (<s>anvita</s>), or rather, come to rest in the connected meaning.

In the case of the words '<s>āditya</s>' and '<s>yūpa</s>,' since their respective meanings established by direct experience are incompatible, the primary signification (<s>mukhyavṛtti</s>) is abandoned.

Thus and so on. But the blessed <s>Yāmunamuni</s> (i.e., <s>Yāmunācārya</s>) has refuted the inference of the speaker's knowledge in [establishing] the validity of scripture. And he has concluded: 'Therefore, in cases such as "There is fruit on the river bank," the cognition that has an established object is verbal (<s>śabdī</s>), not inferential (<s>anumānukī</s>).' This very position has been followed by <s>Varadaviṣṇumiśra</s>.

evaṃ lakṣitalakṣaṇā grāhyā /

children.translated_text: The function based on the second [kind of proximity] is <s>gauṇī</s> (metaphorical usage).

children.text: yathā siṃho devadatta ityatra siṃhmaśabdasya śauryādigūṇaṇyogini devadatte /
children.translated_text: For example, in '<s>Devadatta</s> is a lion,' the word '<s>siṃha</s>' [is applied to] <s>Devadatta</s>, who possesses qualities such as valor and the like.
In the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>, however, it has been stated thus: 'The relation of signifier and signified between word and meaning is thus established.
The relation here is <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation), which is to be understood as twofold: primary and secondary.

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, <s>Śabdādhyāya</s>, section 5. Significatory function (<s>vṛtti</s>) is of two kinds — due to the distinction between primary denotation (<s>abhidhā</s>) and figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>). The significatory function that pertains to the meaning established through linguistic convention (<s>vyutpatti</s>) alone is <s>abhidhā</s> (primary denotation). For example, the word '<s>siṃha</s>' (lion) in [the sense of] the king of beasts. That is of many varieties, due to differences in having universals (<s>jāti</s>), qualities (<s>guṇa</s>), and the like as its objects, and due to the distinction and combination of convention-based usage (<s>yoga</s>) and established usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>). When the primary meaning is obstructed, the significatory function that operates upon what is proximate to it is figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>). And proximity (<s>āsatti</s>) is of two kinds: relation with the primary meaning, and relation with a quality of the primary meaning. Of these, the function based on the former is <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary indication). For example, in 'The cowherd settlement dwells on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' the word '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' [indicates] the bank, which is related to the denoted [meaning], namely the particular flow [of the river]. Similarly, <s>lakṣitalakṣaṇā</s> (indication based on what is indicated) should be understood.
For one who intends to employ a word, [denotation] whose nature is the cognition of the denoted meaning,
That [denotation] which is caused by the power of the word with respect to its own meaning is called primary (<s>mukhyā</s>).
That which operates upon a secondary object through the door of denoting its own [primary] meaning is considered secondary.',
Thus [ends the citation].
The elaboration of that is to be seen in that very [work, the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s>].

children.text:
na ca gauṇalākṣaṇikaprayogayoravācyaviṣayatvādavācyatvam /

children.translated_text: And there would be the undesirable consequence of <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) being exhausted in the word-meaning [alone, leaving no valid means of knowledge for sentence-meaning].
Nor is there mutual dependence (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>) in <s>anvitābhidhāna</s>, since it relies merely on mutual recollection.
As they say: "All the words that are heard, having their connected meanings recalled,
with their particular instances ascertained through reasoning, subsequently give rise to the cognition of the sentence-meaning."

Nor is there non-denotation on account of the domain of <s>gauṇa</s> (secondary) and <s>lākṣaṇika</s> (figurative) usages being that of what is not denoted,
because even though they proceed merely through relation and similarity, they are beginningless;
and precisely for that reason, in the intended context, usage is justified according to propriety.
All these <s>vṛttis</s> (semantic functions) are included within the <s>anvitābhidhāna-vṛtti</s> (the function of expressing connected meaning).
Individual words are merely prompts for recollection.
For in the <s>abhihitānvaya</s> view, one would have to postulate three capacities — the capacity of words for word-meanings, of word-meanings for sentence-meaning (or of parts for the whole meaning), and of words for that [sentence-meaning] — which is a proliferation of postulated capacities; alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence that the sentence-meaning is non-verbal (<s>aśābda</s>).
Thus.

children.text:
nāpi paunaruktyādidoṣaḥ; tattadaṃśapratiniyataśaktitvāt /
nāpi vākyabhedaḥ, ekapradhānatayā svārthābhidhānāt /
"padārtha eva vākyārthaḥ saṃsṛṣṭo hyabhidhīyate" ityuktaṃ /
tathā "nānā śabdādibhedāt" ityādhikaraṇe "yadyapi 'veda' 'upāsīta' ityādayaḥ śabdāḥ pratyayāvṛttyabhidhāyinaḥ, pratyayāśca brahmaikaviṣayāḥ; tathāpi tattatprakaraṇoditajagadekakāraṇatvāpahatapāpmatvādiviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭabrahmaviṣayapratyayāvṛttyavabodhinaḥ pratyayāvṛttirūpā vidyā bhindanti" iti /
vedārthasaṃgrahepi--- "śodhakeṣvapi 'satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma' 'ānando brahma' ityādiṣu sāmānādhikaraṇyavyutpattisiddhānekaguṇaviśiṣṭhaikārthābhidhānamaviruddhamiti sarvaviśiṣṭaṃ brahmaivābhidhīyate" iti /
atraiva pūrvabhāge "samabhivyāhṛtapadāntaravācyānvayayogyamevetarapadapratipādyamityanvitābhidhāyipadasaṃghātarūpavākyaśravaṇasamanantarameva pratīyate /
tacca svargasādhanatvarūpam /
ataḥ kriyāvadananyārthatā virodhādeva parityaktā" iti /
eṣāṃ svārasyamanvitābhidhāne /

children.translated_text: And there is no indication here that this was stated merely by way of concession to the opponent's position (<s>parābhyupagama</s>).

children.text: varadaviṣṇumiśrairapi "satyajñānādipadānāmakhaṇḍaikarasārthatve anvitābhidhānānupapatteśca" ityādiṣu bahuṣu pradeśeṣu anvitābhidhānameva māyāvādinaṃ pratyuktam /
children.translated_text: <s>Varadaviṣṇumiśra</s> also, in many passages such as "because <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> would be impossible if the words <s>satya</s>, <s>jñāna</s>, and so on had an undifferentiated, unitary meaning," has refuted the <s>Māyāvādin</s> (Advaitin) on the basis of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> alone.

And it has been said in the <s>Āgamaprāmāṇya</s>: "Even through [the theory of] expressing connected meaning in other [ways],
since practical usage is justified [only through it],
this [principle of] words expressing connected meaning must necessarily be resorted to."

Nor is there the fault of redundancy and so forth, because the capacity is restricted to each particular component.
Nor is there splitting of the sentence, since the individual meanings are expressed with a single principal purport.
It has been said: "The sentence-meaning is nothing but the word-meaning, for it is the connected [meaning] that is expressed."
Likewise, in the <s>adhikaraṇa</s> (topical section) beginning with "<s>nānā śabdādibhedāt</s>" (on account of difference of words and so on), [it is stated]: "Although words such as 'know' (<s>veda</s>), 'meditate upon' (<s>upāsīta</s>), and the like express recurrence of cognition, and the cognitions have <s>Brahman</s> alone as their object, nevertheless, since they bring about awareness of the recurrence of cognitions whose object is <s>Brahman</s> qualified by specific qualifiers such as being the sole cause of the universe, being free from evil, and so on, as taught in each respective context, the <s>vidyā</s> (meditation), which is of the nature of recurrent cognition, is differentiated."
And in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s> also: "Even in elucidatory [texts] such as '<s>satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma</s>' (Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite) and '<s>ānando brahma</s>' (Brahman is bliss), it is consistent that what is expressed is a single entity qualified by multiple attributes established through the etymological analysis of co-referential terms (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>); thus it is <s>Brahman</s> alone, qualified by all [attributes], that is denoted."
In the earlier portion of that same [work]: "What is to be conveyed by each word is precisely that which is fit for syntactic connection with the meaning expressed by the other co-occurring words — this is understood immediately upon hearing the sentence, which is of the nature of a collection of words expressing connected meaning (<s>anvitābhidhāyin</s>).
And that [meaning so understood] has the nature of being a means to heaven.
Therefore, the [view that the sentence has] no independent purpose beyond the action is abandoned precisely because of the contradiction."
The natural purport of all these [passages] is <s>anvitābhidhāna</s>.
Beginning from that, [it continues]: "Therefore, with regard to [meanings that are] desired, proximate, fit, and connected with other meanings,
the etymological derivation of words in their own meanings should be accepted by all disputants."
In the <s>Tattvaratnākara</s> also: "This [principle of] words expressing connected meaning must necessarily be resorted to;
thus <s>Yāmunācārya</s> taught <s>anvitābhidhā</s> (expression of connected meaning) by words themselves."

Beginning from that, [the position] has been elaborated at length and concluded: "Through six justifications beginning with [the justification from] cognition, with objections refuted, <s>anvitābhidhā</s> (expression of connected meaning) by words is established;
the position of <s>abhihitānvaya</s> (post-denotative connection) does not hold, due to the reversal [of arguments]. Thus everything is consistent."
Thus.
Thus.

And in the <s>Prajñāparitrāṇa</s> and <s>Nyāyasudarśana</s>, it has been stated many times: "The property of words expressing connected meaning is grounded in the capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of words;
its opposite [i.e., <s>abhihitānvaya</s>] arises from a defect in the intellect of one who investigates etymological derivation."
[This was stated] by means of [the verse beginning with] that and so on.
Thus.

children.text:
nanvabhihitānvayadyotakānyapi vākyāni vidyante /
vedārthasaṃgrahe tāvat "evaṃ bodhakānāṃ padasaṃghātānāṃ saṃsargaviśeṣa bodhanena vākyaśabdābhidheyānāmuccāraṇakramo yatra puruṣabuddhipūrvakaḥ" ityādyuktam /

prakṛtipratyayayogena hi padatvam; prakṛtipratyayorarthabhedena padasyaiva viśiṣṭārthapratipādanamavarjanīyam /
children.translated_text: for word-hood arises through the combination of a stem and a suffix; and it is unavoidable that the word itself, through the semantic distinction of stem and suffix, conveys a qualified meaning.
And the distinction of words is grounded in the distinction of meanings.
Because the sentence, which is of the form of a collection of words, denotes the connection of multiple word-meanings along with [their] specific features" — and so on, it has been stated.

children.text: evaṃ vyutpattinirūpaṇe vedārthasaṃgrahe "siddhavastuṣu śabdasya bodhakatvaśaktigrahaṇamatyantasukaram" ityupakramya, "apavarake daṇḍaḥ sthitaḥ" iti vākye yādṛcchikavyutpattiprakāramupapādya, "tathā bālaḥ 'tātoyam, anbaiṣā' ityādinā buddhipūrvavyutpādanena tattatpadānāṃ tattatpadārtheṣveva bodhakatvaśaktigrahaṇamupapādya, punarapi "asya śabdasyāyamartha iti pūrvavṛddhaiḥ śikṣitaḥ" ityādi coktvā, "evameva sarvapadānāṃ svārthābhidhāyitvaṃ saṃghātaviśeṣāṇāṃ ca yathāvasthitasaṃsargaviśeṣavācitvaṃ ca jānāti" ityādyuktam //
children.translated_text: Similarly, in the discussion of etymological derivation (<s>vyutpatti</s>) in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s>, beginning with "the apprehension of the communicative capacity of words with respect to established entities is extremely easy," [the author], having demonstrated the process of natural etymological derivation through the sentence "the stick is standing in the inner room," and having then demonstrated through the phrase "this is father, this is mother" and so on the apprehension of the communicative capacity of each word for its respective meaning through intentional instruction by elders, and having further stated "he was taught by elder wise men that 'this is the meaning of this word,'" it is said: "In this very way, one knows the capacity of all words to denote their own meanings, and the capacity of specific collections [of words] to convey the specific connections as they actually obtain" — and so on.

Objection: But there are also statements that indicate <s>abhihitānvaya</s>.
In the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s>, for instance, it is said: "Thus, for collections of words that are communicative, by communicating a specific connection, the sequential utterance of sentence-words whose denotata are to be expressed is governed by human intention" and so on.
Likewise, in that same [work]: "Because the word itself, in the form of a stem and suffix, contains multiple qualifiers, and because the sentence communicates the connection of multiple word-meanings."
And in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> also: "A word has the capacity to denote an object specifically qualified, precisely because it operates in the form of words and sentences;

children.text:
bhāṣyepi prathamasūtrapūrvapakṣanirākaraṇe--- "evaṃ kila laukikāḥ śabdārthasaṃbandhamavadhārayanti---mātāpitṛprabhṛtibhiḥ ambātātamātulādīn" ityādinā padavyutpattiḥ pūrvamupapāditā /
tatra ca "teṣu teṣvartheṣu teṣāṃ śabdānāṃ prayogo bodhakatvanibandhanaḥ iti niścinvanti" ityādyuktam /
punaśca "vyutpannetaraśabdeṣvasya śabdasyāyamarthaḥ iti pūrvavṛddhaiḥ śikṣitāḥ" ityādi /
children.translated_text: And again: "For one who has acquired competence in other words, [it is ascertained that] 'this is the meaning of this word' — [thus] they were taught by elder wise men" and so on.

children.text: yadināmānvitābhidhānamabhimataṃ; tadā kathamiva padamātre vyutpattiḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: If indeed <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> were the accepted [doctrine], then how could etymological derivation be in a bare word alone?

children.text: yadi ca sā syāt, kathamanvitamabhidheyam, vyutpattivaiparītyaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: And if such [derivation in bare words] were possible, how could connected meaning be what is denoted, since there would be the undesirable consequence of contradiction with the [observed] etymological derivation?

children.text: tasmānnānvitābhidhānameva siddhānta iti nirṇetuṃ śakyam, iti kecit //
children.translated_text: Therefore, it cannot be conclusively determined that <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> alone is the established doctrine — thus say some.

In the <s>Bhāṣya</s> also, in the refutation of the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view) on the first <s>sūtra</s>: "Thus indeed do worldly people ascertain the relation between word and meaning — through mother, father, and others [teaching them] words like '<s>ambā</s>' (mother), '<s>tāta</s>' (father), '<s>mātula</s>' (maternal uncle)" — and so on, the etymological derivation of words was first demonstrated.
And there it was said: "They ascertain that the usage of those words in those meanings is grounded in [their] communicative capacity" and so on.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 6 anye tu "bodhakānām" ityādivākyamanvite saṃsargaviśeṣasiddherupapadyate /
padavākyabhedābhidhānamapi tattadviśeṣavaiśiṣṭyapradarśanamātrārthaṃ, parābhyupagamadyotanārthaṃ vā /
pratyekapadavyutpattyabhidhānamapyanvitārthabodhanopayuktāsādhāraṇadvāraprakāśanamātram /
padārthaṃ smārayitvaiva hi padāni vakyārthaṃ bodhayantītyuktan /
smṛteśca svānubhūtimūlatvānna śaktyantarakḷptiḥ /

children.translated_text: And the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and other [texts] have been explained as having <s>anvita</s> (connected meaning) as their purport by <s>Śrīrāmamiśra</s> in his <s>Vivaraṇa</s> (commentary).

children.text: tathā ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepepi--- "śabdaśca svataḥ śakyamanvitatayā bodhayati, asaṃbhghaverthāntaram, iti hi vyutpattiḥ---" ityādyuktam /
children.translated_text: Likewise, in the <s>Ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepa</s> also: "And a word inherently communicates what it is capable of [denoting] as connected; anything else is impossible — such indeed is the etymological derivation" — and so on, it has been stated.
Therefore, <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> is the established doctrine.

Thus, by the power of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s>, and because the cognition of qualified [entities] cannot be otherwise explained, the capacity of words too to denote qualified [entities] (<s>viśiṣṭābhidhāyitva</s>) is established.

nyā. pa. śa. 6 Others, however, [respond]: The statement beginning with "of those that are communicative" and so on is justified because the specific connection is established in the connected [meaning].
The mention of the distinction between word and sentence is merely for the purpose of showing the particular qualificatory features of each, or for indicating the opponent's accepted position.
The mention of etymological derivation for individual words too is merely the illumination of the distinctive means useful for communicating connected meaning.
For it has been said that words communicate sentence-meaning only after recalling word-meanings.
And since recollection is grounded in one's own prior experience, there is no need to postulate an additional capacity.

children.text: nyā. pa. śa. 7 ata eva viśiṣṭārthābhidhāyitvepi viśeṣaṇamatre śaktiḥ ityapi nirastam; abhidhāyitvātiriktaśaktyantarābhāvāt /

children.translated_text: The statement that [the capacity] does not terminate [at any final referent] is also [refuted], because that which has the capacity to communicate a qualified [entity] cannot rest in the qualifier alone.

children.text: viśiṣṭānupraviṣṭaṃ hi viśeṣaṇaṃ pareparañjakaveṣameveti tādṛgākāro viśeṣyagrahaṇamantareṇa durgrahaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the qualifier, as it enters into the qualified [entity], is like an ornament that embellishes another; such a form [of the qualifier] is difficult to apprehend without apprehending the qualificand (<s>viśeṣya</s>).

children.text: tāvatā ca tadarthaṃ viśeṣyagrahaṇamiti vyarthaṃ vacaḥ /
children.translated_text: And to that extent, to say that the apprehension of the qualificand is for the sake of [understanding] that [qualifier] is a pointless statement.
Because it is proper to establish [the matter] in accordance with how it is actually cognized.

nyā. pa. śa. 7 For precisely this reason, the [view] that even though [words] denote qualified meanings, the capacity resides in the qualifier alone is also refuted — because there is no additional capacity beyond the capacity to denote [the qualified whole].

children.text:
kiṃ ca--- gavādiśabdābhihitagotvādyarthasvabhāvataḥ /
vyaktidhīryadi tadvat syāt niṣkarṣakapadeṣvapi /
gavādiśabdā jātyādīn paratantrān pracakṣate /
tenāśrayapratītiścet tannaḥ siddhaḥ samīhitam /
paraṃ kathamavijñāpya pāratantryasya bodhanam /
vijñāpya yadi śabdasya tatra śaktirna kiṃ bhavet /
parasya paratantreṇa tathā buddhena bodhanam /
tadbuddhyā paratantrasya bodhanenyonyasaṃśrayaḥ /
paradhīnirapekṣaṃ cet pāratantryaṃ pratīyate /
na tena parabuddhiḥ syānniṣkṛṣṭapratipattivat /
pāratantryaṃ svarūpaṃ cet tulyaṃ niṣkarṣakepi tat /
adhikaṃ dharminiṣṭhatvādanyannopalabhāmahe /
padāntaraparāmarśanirapekṣapratītike /
nirūḍhalakṣaṇāvādāḥ paryāyāvṛttigocarāḥ /
vyaktergaurityaniṣkarṣānniṣkarṣe tvādyapekṣaṇāt /
niṣkarṣakeṣvadṛṣṭeśca na jātyā vyaktilakṣaṇā /

children.translated_text: One who maintains that words have their capacity in <s>ākṛti</s> (form/universal) alone —
why does he not accept [that the capacity resides] in <s>sattā</s> (existence) alone for all [words]?
Therefore, from words like '<s>go</s>' and others, the cognition whose object is the qualified [entity]
must be forcefully acknowledged as produced by the capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of the word.

Moreover: If the cognition of the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) from the meaning such as <s>gotva</s> (cowness) denoted by words like '<s>go</s>' (cow) arises from the intrinsic nature [of that meaning], then the same should apply in the case of words that extract [specific referents] as well.
Words like '<s>go</s>' denote <s>jāti</s> (universal) and the like as dependent [on their substrata];
if [you say] the cognition of the substratum [arises] through that [dependence], then what we desire is established.
Without making the superordinate [entity] known, how can its dependence be communicated?
If [you say] it is communicated [after making the superordinate known], then why should the word not have capacity with respect to that [superordinate]?
If the cognition of the superordinate is through [the universal] as known to be dependent, and [simultaneously] the cognition of the dependent [universal] is through the cognition of that [superordinate], there would be mutual dependence.
If [you say] the dependence is cognized independently of the cognition of the superordinate, then through that [alone] there would be no cognition of the superordinate, just as in the case of an extracted cognition.
If [you say] dependence is [part of] the intrinsic nature [of the universal], the same applies equally in the case of extractive [words] too;
we do not perceive anything additional [in the latter case] beyond the fact that [the dependence] resides in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>).
With respect to what is cognized independently of reference to other words,
the claims of <s>nirūḍhalakṣaṇā</s> (conventional secondary signification) apply [only] within the domain of synonymous usage.
The individual is [cognized] from '<s>gauḥ</s>' without extraction; but in extraction, there is dependence on the former [non-extractive cognition].
And since [such dependence] is not observed in extractive [words], the individual is not [denoted] by the universal through <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification).

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 8 yattu "na lokavyutpattihaniḥ, tatraiva śakteḥ" iti ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepe śrīrāmamiśrairuktam, tadapi tatra śaktyabhāvapratikṣepaparam /
asamāptadhīstu vedāntāśruterbhramaḥ /
āpātavyutpattyā śrutestatpūrtirityanantaramabhidhānāt /
yaccātmasiddhau "yathā gavādipadaśaktirekabuddhisiddhepi sāmānyaviśeṣātmake vastuni sāmānyāṃśena saṃbadhyate" iti /
tadapi parābhyupagatodāharaṇamanyārtham /
yatheti parasaṃpratipannanidarśanāt /

children.translated_text: Even for words denoting qualities, by the same reasoning stated for <s>jāti</s>-words (universal-denoting words),
since they denote what is inseparably established (<s>apṛthaksiddha</s>), <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) for the quality-bearer is not appropriate.
When a <s>mantra</s> is elided [in a ritual] due to a specific accent or gender [variation], the ritual modification does not [thereby] apply;
but we do not consider that the <s>viśiṣṭa-vācakatva</s> (capacity to denote the qualified entity) is [thereby] undermined.

nyā. pa. śa. 8 As for what <s>Śrīrāmamiśra</s> said in the <s>Ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepa</s>: "There is no loss of worldly etymological derivation, because the capacity is right there" — that too is aimed at rejecting the absence of capacity there.
But the understanding of one whose knowledge is incomplete [would lead to] a misconception regarding <s>Vedānta</s>.
Because immediately after, it is stated that the superficial derivation is completed by what is heard [in the Vedānta texts].
And as for what is said in the <s>Ātmasiddhi</s>: "Just as the capacity of words like '<s>go</s>' is related through the universal-aspect to an entity that is of the nature of both universal and particular, even when established through a single cognition" —
that too is an illustration conceded to the opponent and serves a different purpose,
since the exemplification is one acknowledged by the opponent, as indicated by the word 'just as' (<s>yathā</s>).

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 9 ato niṣkarṣakaśabdātiriktānāmapṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇavācināṃ viśeṣyaparyavasānavyutpatteḥ śarīravācināṃ devādiśabdānāmapi yathāprayogaṃ śarīriparyavasānaṃ siddham /
ata evacātmapṛthivyādiśabdānāmīśvaraparyantatā /
tena "sarvaṃsvatvidaṃ brahma" "jyotīṃṣi viṣṇuḥ" "ayamātmābrahya" "tattvamasi"ityādisāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tattatprakārakabrahmaparam /
nāmarūpavyākaraṇaṃ ca tadanupraveśāt /
ata eva ca tasya sarvaśabdavācyatvamapi śrūyateth; tadeva ca vyajyate "tadanupraviśya sacca tyaccābhavat" iti /
smaryate ca--- "sarvaṃ samāpnoṣi tatosi sarvaḥ" iti /
sūtritaṃ ca--- "carācaravyapāśrayastu syāt tadvyapadeśo bhāktastadbhāvabhāvitvāt" iti /
uktaṃ ca varadaviṣṇumiśraiḥ--- "svargakāmaśabdena kāmyamānasvargaḥ puruṣobhidhīyate /
na hīśvarovāptasamastakāmaḥ svargaṃ kāmayate, tasyātyalpasukhatvāt /
ato vācyaikadeśe jīve lakṣaṇā, gaṅgāśabdasya tīra iva" iti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) [applies to] the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), which is a part of what is denoted, just as the word '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' [refers] to the bank [rather than the river itself]."

Or alternatively, even words like '<s>svargakāma</s>' and the like have primary denotation (<s>mukhyatva</s>) with respect to the <s>jīva</s> and so on alone, because the ground for their application (<s>pravṛttinimitta</s>) is not abandoned.

children.text: ata eva hi bhāktapadasya bhaktyā vyapadeśārthatvamapi bhāṣyakārairuktam /
children.translated_text: For precisely this reason, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator, i.e., <s>Rāmānuja</s>) also stated that the purpose of the word '<s>bhākta</s>' (figurative) is to indicate that the designation is [applied] through a relation (<s>bhakti</s>).

children.text: viśiṣṭaveṣasya śaktiviṣayatvāt tattyoge kathaṃ na lakṣaṇeti cet, aparityaktapravṛttinimittasya vyutpattyanupraviṣṭamātrabodhanaṃ mukhyatā, tadabhāvakṛta upacāra iti vyavasthānāt //
children.translated_text: If it is asked: since the qualified form (<s>viśiṣṭa-veṣa</s>) is the domain of the word's capacity, how is there no <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) when [the word is applied to] that [qualified entity]? — [the answer is:] because for one whose ground of application is not abandoned, the communication of what is merely included in the etymological derivation is primary denotation (<s>mukhyatā</s>); figuration (<s>upacāra</s>) arises [only] from the absence of that [ground]. This is the settled position.

nyā. pa. śa. 9 Therefore, since for all words other than extractive words, the etymological derivation of those that denote inseparably established qualifiers terminates in the qualificand, it is established that words such as '<s>deva</s>' and the like, which denote the body, also terminate in the embodied self (<s>śarīrin</s>) in accordance with usage.
For precisely this reason, words such as '<s>ātman</s>' (self), '<s>pṛthivī</s>' (earth), and the like ultimately refer to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord).
Consequently, co-referential usages (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) such as "all this is <s>Brahman</s>," "the luminaries are <s>Viṣṇu</s>," "this self is <s>Brahman</s>," and "<s>tat tvam asi</s>" (you are that) all have as their purport <s>Brahman</s> as qualified by their respective qualifiers.
And the differentiation of name and form (<s>nāmarūpavyākaraṇa</s>) [is possible] because of His entering into [all things].
For precisely this reason, His being denoted by all words (<s>sarva-śabda-vācyatva</s>) is also declared in <s>śruti</s>; and that alone is indicated by "having entered into that, He became both the existent and the beyond" (<s>tad anupraviśya sac ca tyac cābhavat</s>).
And it is remembered [in <s>smṛti</s>]: "You pervade all; therefore You are the All" (<s>sarvaṃ samāpnoṣi tato'si sarvaḥ</s>).
And it is stated in a <s>sūtra</s>: "But [this] should apply to [all] moving and non-moving [entities]; however, the designation of that [as Brahman] is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>), because of [the entities'] existence being dependent on that [Brahman]."
And <s>Varadaviṣṇumiśra</s> has said: "By the word '<s>svargakāma</s>' (one who desires heaven), the person who desires heaven is denoted.
For the Lord, who has attained all desires, does not desire heaven, since it [contains] extremely meager happiness.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 10 nanu "tattvamasi" ityatra tvamiti śvetaketumātranirdeśe tadasīti sāmānādhikaraṇyāyogaḥ /
śvetaketuśarīrakeśvaranirdeśe tadābhimukhyenopadeśāyogaḥ /
taduddeśena tvamarthavidhānaṃ cāsiśabdānanvayādinā dūranirastam /
prāptārthatayā nigamanarūpatvepipava viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhedo niṣkarṣaṇīyaḥ /
evam "ahaṃ brahmāsmi" ityādivyapadeśopi durnirvahaḥ /
"jīvenātmanā" ityatrāpyātmaśabdena jīvātmādyabhidhānaṃ ṣāṣyakāravacanaviruddham, jīvena mayetyādivyapadeśāt /
paramātmābhidhāne tu tṛtīyānupapattiḥ, "vyākaravāṇi" ityabhihitatvāt /

children.translated_text: Even with a difference in the action, since the subsequent action is unified with the action expressed by '<s>kṛtvā</s>' (having done) and the like, a different agent is impossible, because it would contradict the requirement of having the same agent [for the absolutive and the main verb].
If the instrumental case is [explained as being applied to] the agent with the intention of expressing instrumentality (<s>karaṇatva</s>), there would be a loss of primary meaning.

children.text: ataścāreṇānupraviśya parabalaṃ saṃkalayānītivajjīvasyavai praviśatikartṛtvam; parastu vyākaraṇamātrakartā /
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as one who, having entered through a spy, makes the enemy's army unite [with one's own forces], the <s>jīva</s> has the agency of entering [into the body]; but the Supreme [Lord] is the agent only of the differentiation [of names and forms].

children.text: tāvatā tu śabdānāṃ na tatparyantatvasiddhiḥ iti //
children.translated_text: But from that much alone, the conclusion that all words ultimately refer to Him is not established — thus [the objection concludes].

nyā. pa. śa. 10 Objection: In "<s>tat tvam asi</s>" (you are that), if the word '<s>tvam</s>' (you) refers merely to <s>Śvetaketu</s>, then the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with '<s>tat asi</s>' (you are that) would be impossible.
If it refers to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) as the inner self of <s>Śvetaketu</s>'s body, then instruction directed toward him [<s>Śvetaketu</s>] would be impossible.
And the alternative of prescribing the meaning of '<s>tvam</s>' for his sake is thoroughly refuted by the non-connection of the word '<s>asi</s>' (are) and other [arguments].
Even if [the sentence] has the character of a concluding restatement (<s>nigamana</s>) because its meaning is already established, the distinction between qualifier and qualificand must still be extracted.
Likewise, the usage in "<s>ahaṃ brahmāsmi</s>" (I am <s>Brahman</s>) and similar [statements] is difficult to account for [on the opponent's view].
In "<s>jīvenātmanā</s>" (by the self which is the <s>jīva</s>) also, denoting the <s>jīvātman</s> and so on by the word '<s>ātman</s>' (self) contradicts the statement of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>, since the usage is "by the <s>jīva</s>, by me" and so on.
But if it denotes the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self), then the instrumental case (<s>tṛtīyā</s>) is unjustified, because [the subject] has [already] been expressed by the verb '<s>vyākaravāṇi</s>' (let me differentiate).

children.text: nyā. pa. śa. 11 atrocyate saṃbuddhistāvadatra ātmavidyopadeśena śvetaketumātraparyavasiteti nāsaṃbodhyasaṃbodhanam /
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, section 11. Here it is stated: The address (<s>saṃbuddhi</s>) in this case is directed solely at <s>Śvetaketu</s> through the teaching of Self-knowledge — hence it is not an address to one who is not to be addressed.
And the specific verbal form is only '<s>tat asi</s>' ('that thou art').
There, co-ordinate predication (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) is justified either through the cause-effect relation, or through the body-soul relation.
In both [interpretations], the word '<s>tvam</s>' (you) too is established as culminating in the substance denoted by the word '<s>tat</s>' (that).
The identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) of something qualified by one attribute with [itself as] qualified by another attribute
is non-difference from itself — [this applies] to the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) and the embodied [soul].

children.text:
atastvaccharīrakaṃ brahmeti vivakṣāyāṃ satyāṃ tvaṃ taditi nirdeśamātramupapannam /
madhyamapuruṣaśca tvaṃśabdaprayoganibandhanaḥ, "yuṣmadyupapade samānādhikaraṇe sthāninyapi madhyamaḥ" iti vidhānāt /
ataḥ sopi tvaṃśabdaparyavasānaviṣayaparyavasitaḥ /
yadvā tat tvamasītyevānvayostu /
na coddeśyānuguṇā tiṅvibhaktiriti niyamaḥ, upādeyānuguṇaliṅgavacanādinirdeśavadatrāpi virodhābhāvāt /
prayuñjate ca patañjaliprabhṛtaya upādeyānuguṇāmapi tiṅvibhaktim--- "sa punarāvṛttaḥ suvarṇapiṇḍaḥ khadirāṅgārasavarṇe kuṇḍale bhavataḥ" ityādiṣu /
etena "ahaṃ brahmāsmi" ityādikamapi nirvyūḍham /
"jīvenātmānā" ityatrāpyanena nyāyena svaśabdaparyāyeṇātmaśabdena jīvaśabdasya sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tāvat siddham /

children.translated_text: And the inapplicability of the instrumental case (third case-ending) is equally [a problem] on both the view of identity of essential nature and the view of separateness.

children.text: athāṃśabhedādinā vibhajya karaṇatvādivivakṣayā kathañcinnirvāhaḥ, tathā viśiṣṭākārādibhedavivakṣayā vibhajyātrāpi nirvāhamanumanyethāḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, if [you say] there is some resolution by dividing through distinctions of part and so forth, and by intending instrumentality and the like, then you should also accept that here too there is resolution by dividing through distinctions of qualified form and the like.
Therefore, in sentences of <s>Śruti</s> and so forth, when contradictory meanings are connected,
co-ordinate predication does not rest upon essential identity of nature.

Therefore, when the intended meaning is '<s>Brahman</s> has you as its body' — the mere indication '<s>tvam tat</s>' ('you [are] that') is appropriate. And the second person [verbal form] is occasioned by the use of the word '<s>tvam</s>' (you), by the rule: 'even when the substitute is in co-ordinate predication with a word in the second-person reference (<s>yuṣmad</s>), [the verb takes] the second person.' Therefore, it too culminates in the referent in which the word '<s>tvam</s>' terminates. Or alternatively, let the syntactic connection be simply '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('that thou art'). Nor is there a rule that the verbal person-ending must conform to the referent [being addressed]; just as gender, number, and similar [features] are expressed conforming to the predicate (<s>upādeya</s>), so too here there is no contradiction. And <s>Patañjali</s> and others employ verbal person-endings conforming to the predicate — as in 'That lump of gold, having been reworked, becomes (<s>bhavataḥ</s>) two earrings the color of <s>khadira</s> embers,' and the like. By this, '<s>ahaṃ brahmāsmi</s>' ('I am <s>Brahman</s>') and similar [statements] are also explained. In '<s>jīvenātmānā</s>' ('by the soul as the self') as well, by this very principle, the co-ordinate predication of the word '<s>jīva</s>' with the word '<s>ātman</s>' — which is a synonym for '<s>sva</s>' (one's own [self]) — is established.
From being an effect, from inseparable establishment (<s>apṛthaksiddhi</s>), from pervading (<s>āviśa</s>), from resemblance (<s>anukāra</s>),
from existence, creation, utility, and the like — [arises] the cognition of co-ordinate predication.

children.text: na ca tvaddṛṣṭaḥ puruṣaḥ sthāṇuritivat "puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam" "tattvamasi" ityādau bādhārthaṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyamiti vācyam, mukhyavṛttisaṃbhave tadayogāt, prapañcasatyatvādeścābādhitapratyakṣādibalasiddhatvāt /
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said that, just as in your [Advaitin's] view 'the person is a post,' co-ordinate predication in '<s>puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam</s>' ('the person alone is all this') and '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('that thou art') is for the purpose of sublation (<s>bādha</s>) — because when a primary meaning (<s>mukhyavṛtti</s>) is possible, that [sublation-interpretation] is inappropriate; and because the reality of the manifest world and the like is established by the force of uncontradicted perception and other [means of knowledge].

children.text: cidaṃśasāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ tu na bādhasaham, tvayāpi tatsatyatvābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: Co-ordinate predication with respect to the consciousness-aspect (<s>cidaṃśa</s>), however, does not bear sublation, since even you accept the reality of that [consciousness].

children.text: svarūpaikyavidhāne ca viruddhadharmapratirodhāt, tatparityāge padayoranatiriktārthatayā paryāyapadasāmānādhikaraṇyaprasaṅgāt, dvārābhāvena mukhyavṛttibādhāpatteḥ, gatyantare ca saṃbhavati tadayogāt, svarūpamātranirdeśe ca padāntaravaiyarthyāt, svarūpabhedasya ca bahupramāṇasiddhatvāt //
children.translated_text: And if essential identity is asserted — because of the obstruction by contradictory attributes; because if those [attributes] are abandoned, the words [would have] no additional referent, leading to the absurd consequence of co-ordinate predication of synonymous words; because in the absence of a mediating [factor], the primary meaning would be contradicted; because when another interpretation is available, that [identity-interpretation] is inappropriate; because if mere essential nature is denoted, additional words would be purposeless; and because the difference of essential natures is established by many means of valid knowledge.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 12 "satyaṃ jñānam---" ityādilakṣaṇavākyamapi satyatvādiviśiṣṭaikaviṣayam, tathaiva sāmānādhikaraṇyavyutpatteḥ /
na cātra viśeṣaṇabhedādviviśeṣyabhedāprasaṅgaḥ, viruddhaviśeṣaṇābhāvāt; na hi ghaṭapaṭādiṣviva virodhaḥ /
yathā ca pratyakṣe nīlatvotpalatvāderavirodho darśanabalāt, tathātrāpi /
na ca satyatvajñānatvādervaiyadhikaraṇyaniyamo dṛṣṭaḥ, yena virodhaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: Nor is any invariable rule observed that truth-ness and knowledge-ness must belong to different substrates, such that there would be contradiction.

children.text: viśeṣyaikyapare tu sāmānādhikaraṇye viśeṣaṇānāṃ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyayośca mitho bhedo guṇa eva /
children.translated_text: In co-ordinate predication that is directed toward the unity of the qualified, the difference among the qualifiers, and between qualifier and qualified, is merely secondary (<s>guṇa</s>).

Nor does [this entail] the absurd consequence that, just as there is unity of the qualified, there would be unity of qualifier and qualified, or unity among the qualifiers — because of the fault of contradiction with the definition [of co-ordinate predication], and because of non-derivation in that manner.

children.text: nāpi viśiṣṭe viśiṣṭāntaravidhānādviśeṣaṇānāṃ mithaḥ samavāyādidoṣaḥ, yugapadanekaviśiṣṭaikābhidhānāt, anūdya vidhāneṣvapi yathā vyutpatti dharmapradhānatvācca //
children.translated_text: Nor is there the fault of inherence-relation (<s>samavāya</s>) and the like among the qualifiers [merely] because one qualified entity is asserted as qualified by another [set of qualifiers] — because multiple qualifications of a single [entity] are expressed simultaneously; and because even in cases where something is stated after being mentioned [previously], the etymology is consistent, and [the statement] is dominated by the property [being predicated].

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, section 12. The definitional sentence '<s>satyaṃ jñānam</s>...' ('truth, knowledge...') and the like too has a single referent qualified by truth and the like, since co-ordinate predication is understood in precisely that way. Nor is there here the absurd consequence that difference of qualifiers entails difference of the qualified — because there are no mutually contradictory qualifiers; for there is no contradiction [among them] as there is among pot, cloth, and the like. And just as in perception, the non-contradiction of blueness, lotus-ness, and so on is [established] by the force of observation, so too here.

children.text: nyā. pa. śa. 13 na ca viśeṣaṇaṃ sarvaṃ viśeṣaṇāntarāsaham, virodhimātravirodhitvāt, anyathā pratyakṣavirodhāt sādhyasādhakadharmādiviśiṣṭaviṣayānumānādyanudayaprasaṅgāt, evantvādidaṃ viśiṣṭabodhakaṃ na bhavatītyādi vyavahārasyāpi vilopaḥ syāt /
na ca śabdane pratipādane tathā, aviśeṣāt, pratyakṣādivacchabdenāpi yathāvastu bodhanīyatvāt /
children.translated_text: Nor is it so with respect to verbal expression — because there is no distinction [between words and other means of knowledge], since through words too, things are to be communicated as they are, just as through perception and so forth.

children.text: viśeṣaṇamātraparatvaṃ tu nābhyupagatameva, yena viśiṣṭaikyāsiddhiḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: The view that [words] are directed solely toward qualifiers is not even accepted [by us], such that there would be non-establishment of the qualified unity.

children.text: yasya tu viśeṣyamātraparatvaṃ, tasya paryāyatulyatvāt padāntaravaiyarthyalakṣaṇabhaṅgalakṣaṇādidoṣaḥ, pravṛttinimittānāṃ viśeṣaṇānāṃ tyāgāt, viśeṣyamātrasya ca dvārarahitasyālakṣyatvāt /
children.translated_text: But for one who [holds] that [words] are directed solely toward the qualified (<s>viśeṣya</s>) — for him, since it becomes equivalent to synonymy, there is the fault of purposelessness of additional words, breakdown of the definition, and so on — because the causes of [a word's] application, which are the qualifiers, are abandoned, and because the mere qualified [entity], lacking a mediating [factor], cannot be characterized.

children.text: itaravyāvṛttīnāṃ tūpalakṣaṇatve svarūpatve ca padāntaravaiyarthyādidoṣaḥ sa eva //
children.translated_text: And if exclusions from others (<s>itaravyāvṛtti</s>) are held to be either indicatory markers (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) or essential natures — that very same fault of purposelessness of additional words and the like [applies].

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, section 13. Nor is every qualifier unable to coexist with another qualifier — because only what is [genuinely] contradictory is contradictory. Otherwise, from contradiction with perception, there would be the absurd consequence of the non-arising of inference and other [means of knowledge] whose objects are qualified by properties such as 'to be established,' 'establishing,' and the like; and even the common usage 'but this [combination of] qualifiers does not produce a cognition of a qualified entity' and so on would be destroyed.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 14 evaṃ tāsāṃ viśeṣaṇatve pakṣāntaravadviśiṣṭabhedādidoṣastvadukta āpatet, na cennānyatrāpi /
tyaktapravṛttinimittasya tadvirodhivyāvṛttyabhilāṣastvālokamapahāya timiranirākaraṇavāñchā /
vipratipannaṃ vākyamakhaṇḍaparam, samānādhikaraṇavākyatvāt, soyaṃ devadattaḥ iti vākyavat, yadvā lakṣaṇavākyatvāt, prakṛṣṭaprakāśaścandraḥ ityādivat iti cenna, dṛṣṭāntāsiddheḥ, tattedantāviśiṣṭasyaiva devadattasya soyamiti pratīteḥ /
yugapat tayorvyāghāta iti cenna, yaugapadyasyānabhidhānāt, anākṣepācca /
yugapat pratipattistu na doṣaḥ, anyathā pratyabhijñābhaṅge kṣaṇabhaṅganairātmyāpalāpādivādā vijayeran /
tathāpyatītatvavartamānatve kathamekasya ? iti cet, svapradhvaṃsakāle hi svayamatītaḥ syāt, na cāsau pradhvastaḥ, vartamānatvopalaṃbhāt; atītopādhiviśeṣasaṃbandhitayā hi tattvam, na tvatītatayā /
kathamekaṃ pūrvamaparaṃ ca ? iti cenna, pratibandhyupādhibhedenobhayopapatteḥ, anyathā kṣaṇasyāpi pūrvāparamadhyavartinaḥ kṣodaprasaṅgāt; na hi tasya pūrvasmādapi pūrvatvameva, uttarasmādapyuttaratvameva vā /
kṣudyatāṃ kṣaṇopīti cenna, sarvāpahnavaprasaṅgāt, iti /
tiṣṭhattvetat; dvitīyopi dṛṣṭānto viśiṣṭapara eva, anyathā vyāvṛttapratītyanudayaprasaṅgāt, prakṛṣṭatvādiviśeṣaṇavaiyarthyācca /
evaṃ śrutibādhopyanumānayorvaktavyaḥ, paryāyatulyatvādiprasaṅgalakṣaṇapratikūlatarkaśca /
tathā vipratipannaṃ vākyaṃ viśiṣṭaparam, ākāṅkṣāyuktavākyatvāt, vyadhikaraṇavākyavat, iti bādhakamanumānamapi, pratipattyanurodhāt dṛṣṭāntasiddheścāsya balīyastvam /
bhinnapravṛttinimittānāṃ śabdānāmekasminnarthe vṛttiḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyamiti śābdairevoktam /
tatra bhinnapravṛttinimittānāmiti paryāyavyāvṛttiḥ /
ekasminniti vyadhikaraṇānāṃ ghaṭaḥ paṭaityādyananvitānāṃ ca vyavacchedārtham /
śabdānām arthe iti ca vyaktyarthameva, arthe iti viśeṣyasya pradhānatayā vācyatvasūcanārthaṃ vā /
tena vyadhikaraṇavākyeṣvekapradhānārthe vṛttisaṃbhavepiva tasya viśeṣyatavabhāvād vyavacchedyatā /
viśeṣyabodhanavyāpāro vṛttiḥ pravṛttiriti ca sāmānyato viśeṣataścātrocyate /

children.translated_text: For <s>pravṛtti</s> (operation/activity) is the preeminent <s>vṛtti</s> (function).
And the preeminence here is by virtue of having the qualified as its object.

children.text: tatra yadupādhikā viśeṣye śabdavṛttiḥ, tat pravṛttinimittam /
children.translated_text: There, that [property] by which the word functions with respect to the qualified is the cause of its application (<s>pravṛttinimitta</s>).
The expression of a single qualified entity through different qualifiers is co-ordinate predication — this is what is stated.

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, section 14. Thus, if those [exclusions] are held as qualifiers, the fault of difference of the qualified and so forth — as stated by you for other positions — would apply. And if not [for us], then not for others either. One who, having abandoned the causes of application [of a word], desires exclusion from what contradicts them — [that is like] one who, turning away from light, desires the removal of darkness. [Objection:] The contested sentence is directed toward an undivided [reality], because it is a sentence with co-ordinate predication — like the sentence '<s>sa ayaṃ Devadattaḥ</s>' ('this is that <s>Devadatta</s>'); or because it is a definitional sentence — like '<s>prakṛṣṭaprakāśaś candraḥ</s>' ('the moon is of eminent luminosity'). [Reply:] No, because the example is not established — for it is <s>Devadatta</s> himself, qualified by 'that-ness' and 'this-ness,' who is recognized in '<s>sa ayam</s>' ('this is that one'). [Objection:] There is contradiction between the two [qualifications] simultaneously. [Reply:] No, because simultaneity is not what is denoted [by the sentence], and because there is no implication [of simultaneity]. [Objection:] But simultaneous cognition is [problematic]. [Reply:] No, it is not a fault; otherwise, if recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) were destroyed, doctrines of momentariness, no-self, and denial would prevail. [Objection:] Still, how can one [entity] be both past and present? [Reply:] At the time of its own cessation it would be past — but it has not ceased, because its present-ness is perceived; for its reality consists in its relation to the particular limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of the past, not in being past [as such]. [Objection:] How can one thing be both earlier and later? [Reply:] There is no [difficulty], because both are justified through difference in the obstructing limiting adjuncts; otherwise, even a moment, occupying earlier, later, and middle positions, would be subject to fragmentation — for it is not the case that it is only earlier than the earlier, or only later than the later. [Objection:] Then let the moment too be fragmented! [Reply:] No, because that would lead to the denial of everything. Let this stand. The second example too is directed toward the qualified; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of non-arising of the cognition of exclusion, and the purposelessness of qualifiers like 'eminence' and the like. Similarly, the sublation of <s>Śruti</s> [statements] by the two [opposing] inferences should be addressed, along with the unfavorable reasoning characterized by the absurd consequence of equivalence with synonyms and the like. Furthermore, the inference 'the contested sentence is directed toward the qualified, because it is a sentence with co-ordinate predication, like a sentence with words in different grammatical substrates (<s>vyadhikaraṇa</s>)' — this [counter-]inference too is stronger, because it conforms to cognition and because the example is established. As stated by the grammarians themselves: 'The application of words with different causes of usage to a single referent is co-ordinate predication.' There, 'with different causes of usage' excludes synonyms. 'To a single [referent]' is for excluding words in different substrates such as 'pot' and 'cloth' that are not syntactically connected, as well as [connected sentences predicated of different things]. 'Of words, to the referent' — [the word 'referent'] is for the purpose of [indicating] the particular individual; or the word 'to the referent' is to indicate that the qualified (<s>viśeṣya</s>) is what is primarily denoted. Therefore, even in sentences with words in different substrates, where application to a single primary referent is possible, [that sentence] is excluded [from sāmānādhikaraṇya] because of the absence of the qualified-status [of the referent]. The operation (<s>vṛtti</s>) or activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) [of a word] as communicating the qualified is stated both in general and in particular here.

children.text:
nyā. pa. śa. 15 nanu pauruṣeyaṃ sarvamanvitārthamiti pratipāditam, tannopapadyate, guṇavadvaktṛpraṇītasyaiva vākyasya tathātvadarśanāt, iti cenna, svataḥ prāmāṇyāt, svarasato hi sarvaṃ jñānasabādhitavyavahārajanakaṃ dṛśyate /
bhedāgrahādiviśeṣopādhikaṃ hi kvacid bādhyavyavahārahetutvam /
tataḥ svābhāvikamapi prāmāṇyaṃ pratibandhakena doṣeṇa kvacidapahnutam; yathāgnerauṣṇyam /
tatra tadaṃśāpekṣayā prāmāṇyameva /
guṇāstu saṃbhāvitadoṣasthale doṣanirākaraṇaupayikāḥ, pramāṇyasya tairvyāptyabhāvāt, nityasarvajñavādināṃ pramāṇabhūte tajjñāne vyabhicārāt /
aprāmāṇyasya tu doṣādhīnatvamavyabhicaritānvayavyatirekasiddham /
avastunoprāmāṇyasya kathaṃ hetusādhyatvamiti cenna, saṃśayatvaviparyayatvādirūpasya tasyāvastutvābhāvāt, bhāvāntarātiriktasya cābhāvasyāsmābhiranabhyupagamāt, abhyupagamepi pradhvaṃsasya mudgarādisādhyatvadṛṣṭeḥ /
tadvat pramāpi samyaṅmithyābodhasādhāraṇādatiriktasahitā jāyate, kāryatve sati tadviśeṣatvāt, apramāvat; prāmāṇyaṃ parato jñāyate, anabhyāsadaśāyāṃ sāṃśayikatvāt, aprāmāṇyavat, iti cet, tatra prathame kṛtsnapramāpakṣīkāre hetoḥ svamate bhāgāsiddhirḥ, iśvarapramāyā nityatvābhyupagamāt /
anīśvarapramāpakṣīkāre yāvadīśvarasiddhi vyarthaṃ viśeṣaṇam /
riśvarānumānasamanantaraṃ prayogaḥ iti cenna, tasya śāstrayonyadhikaraṇanyāyenānumātumaśakyatvāt /
tarhi viśeṣaṇaṃ na prayokṣyāmahe iti cenna, svābhimateśvarapramayānaikāntyāt /
anabhyupagateśvaraiḥ saugatādibhirevaṃ prayoge kaḥ parihāraḥ iti cenna, śrutisiddhanityapramāsamarthanena bādhasyānaikāntikasya vā vaktuṃ śakyatvāt /
śrutisiddhanityapramāvyavacchedena kāryatvaviśeṣaṇaṃ saphalaṃ syāt hi cet, tarhi śrutyā tatsiddhiḥ śrutiprāmāṇyanirṇayamantareṇa kathaṃ syāt ? /
tatprāmāṇyaṃ ca nityanirdeṣatayābhyupagamyate cet, kathaṃ tatra parataḥ prāmāṇyetpattiḥ ? vaktṛguṇādhīnaṃ vākyānāṃ prāmāṇyamiti hi vaḥ siddhāntaḥ /
nirdeṣataiva guṇaḥ, iti tadadhīnatayā tatra parataḥ prāmāṇyamiti cenna, pratibandhakābhāvasya paraiḥ kāraṇatvānabhyupagamāt /
abhyupagame ca tāvanmātradhīnatvepi vedāpauruṣeyatvanityatvāderavirodhāt; vedapauruṣeyatvādisiddhyarthaṃ hi vaḥ parataḥ prāmāṇyasamarthanārambhaḥ /
tadapauruṣeyatvādisiddhyarthameva cāsmābhiḥ svataḥ prāmāṇyaṃ pratipādyate /
athāptoktatayā vedaprāmāṇyādīśvarasiddhau tatpramāvyavacchedāya viśeṣaṇamitīṣyate, tadapi na, parataḥ prāmāṇye nirṇīte vadesyāptamūlaprāmāṇyasiddhiḥ, tatsiddhau ceśvarasiddhiḥ, tatpramāvyavacchedāya viśeṣaṇam, saviśeṣaṇaśvāsau hetuḥ parataḥ prāmāṇyaṃ sādhayet, iti cakrakāśrayaprasaṅgārt /
iśvarānumānānyathāsiddhiparihārāya parataḥ prāmāṇyaṃ nyāyakusumāñjalau samarthyate /
tatraiva ca kāryatvaviśeṣaṇaṃ prayujyate /
na cāsiddhivyavacchedāya viśeṣaṇaṃ yuktam; siddhatve tu parataḥ prāmāṇyasamarthanasya na tadarthateti dustaratā /
tathāpi śabdaprāmāṇyaṃ vaktṛguṇādhīnamiti cenna, viśeṣakābhāvāt, doṣasaṃbhāvanāsthale ca tadapekṣaṇāt, vedasya canirdeṣatvāt /
doṣābhāvādhīnatve parataḥ prāmāṇyaṃ siddhamiti cenna, tadadhīnatvābhāvāt, tasya virodhanivṛttimātrarūpatvāt /
astu vā tadadhīnatvam, tathāpi vede tu na doṣaḥ /
guṇamantareṇa doṣābhāvo na ghaṭata iti cet, anuṣṇāśītasparśavadubhayanivṛtterapi darśanāt, upapatteśca /
bhāvāntarābhāvavādino doṣābhāvopi guṇa eveti cenna, svābhāvāntareṇa tannirvāhāt /
children.translated_text: For one who holds that absence is not a separate positive entity — [even] the absence of defects is just a quality [i.e., positive property]. [Reply:] No, because that [absence of defects] is accomplished by a [property] other than [the positive quality] itself.

children.text: na hi tasyāpi śītābhāva uṣṇa eva, anuṣṇāśīte tadasiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: For the absence of coldness in that [anuṣṇāśīta — 'neither hot nor cold'] is not just heat — since that [identity] is not established in what is neither hot nor cold.
For by the inclusion of both [in the negation], it is [characterized as] the absence of coldness [as well].

children.text: tadvadatrāpi saguṇeṣvāptavākyeṣu vaktṛguṇarahiteṣu vedavākyeṣu ca doṣābhāvaḥ samānaḥ //
children.translated_text: Similarly here too, the absence of defects is the same in sentences of trustworthy speakers that possess [positive] qualities and in Vedic sentences that are devoid of a speaker's qualities.

<s>Nyāyapariśuddhi</s>, section 15. Objection: It has been established that all [discourse] of human origin (<s>pauruṣeya</s>) has connected meaning — [but] this is not justified, since only a sentence composed by a speaker possessing good qualities is observed to be so. [Reply:] No, because of intrinsic validity (<s>svataḥ prāmāṇya</s>). For all cognition is spontaneously observed to produce uncontradicted practical activity. Occasional [production of] contradicted practical activity is conditioned by particular [factors] such as non-apprehension of difference, and so forth. Therefore, even natural validity is occasionally concealed by an obstructing defect — just as the heat of fire [is sometimes concealed]. There, with respect to that aspect, validity [remains] as such. Qualities [of the speaker] are useful for removing defects in cases where defects are suspected — since there is no invariable concomitance between validity and those [qualities], as seen from the deviation [of the rule] in the case of the cognition of an eternally omniscient being, which is a valid means of knowledge even for those who hold [such a being exists]. But the dependence of invalidity upon defects is established through invariable positive and negative concomitance without deviation. [Objection:] How can invalidity, being a non-entity (<s>avastu</s>), have a cause or be provable? [Reply:] No, because that [invalidity], being of the form of doubt, error, and the like, is not a non-entity; and because we do not accept absence (<s>abhāva</s>) as something over and above positive entities; and even if [absence] is accepted, destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>) is observed to be producible by hammers and the like. [Objection:] Similarly, valid cognition too arises together with [properties] additional to those common to both correct and erroneous cognition — since, when it is an effect, it is a specific [type of cognition], like invalid cognition. [And:] Validity is known from an extraneous source (<s>parataḥ</s>), because in the stage of non-habituation it is of a doubtful character, like invalidity. [Reply:] To the first [argument]: in our view there is partial non-establishment of the reason, since we accept the eternality of God's cognition, when [the argument] seeks to include all valid cognitions [as produced]. If [the argument] excludes God's cognition, the qualifier 'when it is an effect' is purposeless until God is [first] established. [Objection:] The argument is employed immediately after the inference of God. [Reply:] No, because [God] cannot be inferred by the principle of the <s>Śāstrayoni</s>-<s>adhikaraṇa</s> (i.e., God is known from scripture, not inference alone). [Objection:] Then we will not employ the qualifier. [Reply:] No, because of the non-conclusiveness (<s>anaikāntya</s>) [of the reason] with respect to God's cognition as accepted by you. [Objection:] What is the refutation when Buddhists and others who do not accept God employ this argument? [Reply:] Because [we] can respond by establishing the eternally valid cognition established by <s>Śruti</s>, and [can show] that the sublation [of this] or the non-conclusiveness [of their reason] can be stated. [Objection:] If the qualifier 'being an effect' would be fruitful by excluding the eternally valid cognition established by <s>Śruti</s> — then how can that [eternal cognition] be established by <s>Śruti</s> without [first] determining the validity of <s>Śruti</s>? And if the validity [of <s>Śruti</s>] is accepted as being established by its being free from defects (<s>nirdoṣatā</s>), then how can validity arise from an extraneous source in that case? For your established doctrine is that the validity of sentences depends on the qualities of the speaker. [Objection:] Freedom from defects alone is the quality, and validity depends on that — hence it is extrinsic there too. [Reply:] No, because the opponents do not accept the mere absence of an obstructing factor as a cause. And even if [they did] accept it, there would still be no contradiction with the authorlessness (<s>apauruṣeyatva</s>), eternality, and the like of the <s>Vedas</s>, even though [validity] depends on just that much; for your effort to establish extrinsic validity is for the purpose of establishing the <s>Veda's</s> human authorship and the like. And it is precisely for establishing its authorlessness and the like that intrinsic validity is demonstrated by us. [Objection:] If validity of the <s>Veda</s> is established from its being spoken by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>), and from that God is established, and a qualifier [in the inference] is [needed] to exclude His cognition — then that too is not [correct], because: extrinsic validity being established → the <s>Veda's</s> validity as rooted in a trustworthy speaker is established → God is established → the qualifier excluding His cognition [is employed] → and that very reason with the qualifier would establish extrinsic validity — this leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (<s>cakraka</s>). [Reply:] In the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>, extrinsic validity is established in order to refute the 'otherwise-establishment' (<s>anyathāsiddhi</s>) of the inference for God. And there indeed the qualifier 'being an effect' is employed. But it is not proper to use a qualifier for excluding what is [already] established [through other means]; and if it is [already] established, the effort to establish extrinsic validity is not directed toward that — hence [the objection] is insuperable. [Objection:] Still, the validity of words depends on the qualities of the speaker. [Reply:] No, because there is no differentiating factor; and because in cases where defects are suspected, that [quality] alone is looked for; and because the <s>Veda</s> is free from defects. [Objection:] If [validity] depends on the absence of defects, then extrinsic validity is established. [Reply:] No, because there is no dependence on that, since that [absence of defects] is merely the form of the removal of an obstruction. [Objection:] Let there be such dependence; still, in the case of the <s>Veda</s>, there is no defect.

children.text: nyā. pa. śa. 16 nanu śabdānāṃ svataḥ prāmāṇye buddhādivākyamapi svataḥ pramāṇaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: <s>Nyā. Pa.</s> Section 16. Now, if words have intrinsic validity (<s>svataḥ prāmāṇya</s>), then even the statements of the <s>Buddha</s> and others would be intrinsically valid.

children.text: na syāt, svatastvasyotsargarūpatvāt, virodhiviśeṣe ca tasyānanupraveśāt /
children.translated_text: They would not be, because intrinsic [validity] is of the nature of a general rule (<s>utsarga</s>), and because it does not extend to cases where a specific contradiction [exists].

children.text: uktaṃ cāgamaprāmāṇye--- "naiva śabde svato doṣāḥ prāmāṇyaparipanthinaḥ /
children.translated_text: And it has been stated regarding the validity of scripture (<s>āgama</s>): 'There are no defects in words themselves that obstruct their validity;
rather, it is established that validity belongs to them intrinsically.
In certain cases the mind is shaken by defects in the speaker's intention —
as in [absurd statements like] "a herd of elephants on the tip of a finger" and so forth.'
Thus.
